list 2 of 3Flydubai co-pilot plotted ‘suicide’ attack on Israel, UAE says

list 3 of 3Air France says it will follow Israeli rule barring crew from some nations

end of list

Bulgaria’s Ministry of Defence said an air force MiG-29 fighter jet escorted the plane to Sofia airport.

Initial information showed the aircraft carried six crew members and 51 passengers, all of whom have all since disembarked, according to the Transport Ministry’s statement.

The airline told the AFP news agency that a security search of the aircraft was conducted.

“Once the search of the aircraft is complete, the passengers will be rebooked onto alternative flights as quickly as possible,” the airline said.

A crisis response team has been set up, and relevant authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, the Bulgarian Transport Ministry said.

According to aviation and flight tracking site FlightAware, Austrian Airlines 82 left the Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday at 6:46pm local time (15:46 GMT) and landed about three hours later at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia at 9:43pm (18:43 GMT).

Flightradar24 data showed it entered Romanian airspace at about 9:10pm (18:10 GMT) before turning south and heading back towards Bulgaria.

Information from the flight-tracking platform ADS-B Exchange indicates the aircraft was transmitting squawk code 7700 – a signal for a general emergency – at around the same time.

Flydubai incident

Last month, a Flydubai plane carrying 174 passengers was on its way from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv when a co-pilot allegedly attacked the pilot with an axe in an attempt to crash the plane.

The aircraft plunged about 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control by other Flydubai pilots after passengers and other crew subdued the alleged attacker.

The flight was diverted and forced to make an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Authorities in the UAE said the co-pilot was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.

The co-pilot, Hamam Al-Hammami, an Omani national, has since been charged with terrorism offences in the UAE.

The Israeli government responded to the incident by ordering checks on the identities of all pilots flying into the country.

title: Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader
text:
An alliance of Venezuelan opposition parties has reaffirmed its commitment to exiled Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado as its leader.

On Sunday, members of the opposition’s Unitary Democratic Platform (PUD) agreed in a meeting in Caracas to “recognise and support the leadership of Maria Corina Machado”.

The coalition also renewed its demand for free elections in Venezuela, following a series of contested presidential votes in 2024 and 2018.

Sunday’s statement included 14 proposals for a democratic transition, including freedom for political parties, the release of all political prisoners and the safe return of those who went into exile.

The announcement also increases pressure on authorities to allow Machado’s return. She has been living in exile since leaving Venezuela last December to receive her Nobel Prize.

“The will of the Venezuelans must once again govern the destiny of our nation,” the opposition’s former presidential candidate Edmundo Gonzalez wrote on social media supporting the proposals.

“We will not accept political prisoners, persecution or a governing power that disregards the mandate of its citizens. Living in freedom and under a genuine constitutional order is a legitimate demand of our society.”

No election set

Venezuela has yet to declare a date for a new presidential vote. Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV).

PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture.

Still, after the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV has remained in power with the support of the White House.

US President Donald Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president.

His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms.

But critics point out that Trump has been reluctant to push Rodriguez for new elections, opting instead for a three-phase plan that focuses first on stabilising the country and economic recovery before pursuing a political transition.

Machado, meanwhile, has told The Financial Times she would like to see Venezuela hold elections by July next year.

“The US government and the Venezuelan people all agree ⁠⁠that the only way to make ⁠⁠this sustainable and ⁠⁠a real victory is to turn Venezuela into a stable democracy,” she told the newspaper earlier this month.

title: Alberta independence referendum: Will separatists survive a loss?
text:
Cory Morgan has spent more than 25 years fighting for Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta to become an independent country. On Monday, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the issue for the very first time. But even if the answer is no, Morgan said he’s in it for the long haul.

“I would respect the will of the voters,” he told Al Jazeera. “If they’ve decided it’s not time to go that route yet, then so be it. But that doesn’t mean I’ll stop.”

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

list 1 of 4Canada to fast track oil pipeline meant to diversify economy away from US

list 2 of 4Secessionist party wins Quebec election in Canada

list 3 of 4Canada’s Carney calls for unity as Alberta prepares for secession vote

list 4 of 4Fire at Canadian military base kills at least four, injures dozens

Morgan, the founder of the advocacy organisation Pathway to Independence, is among a group of longtime separatists who have managed to push what was once a fringe idea onto the ballot.

Monday’s provincial referendum asks Alberta residents to weigh whether they would like to pursue a binding resolution in the future on the question of independence.

Polls indicate the pro-independence side has little chance of succeeding, with four of five people in the province saying they want Alberta to remain a part of Canada. But Morgan’s focus is on the one in five who don’t.

“That’s not a movement that’s leaving,” he said.

What the referendum will mean for the separatist movement and for Canada as a whole, however, is a more complicated question.

What exactly are Albertans voting on?

Monday’s ballot gives Albertans two options: to remain part of Canada or begin the legal process for holding a future referendum on separation.

A vote in favour of the second option doesn’t mean Alberta immediately becomes an independent country.

Any province that tries to secede would first have to go through complex negotiations with the federal government in Ottawa, other provinces and Indigenous peoples who live in and around Alberta.

Some separatist organisers have been using that distinction to encourage people to vote for the referendum — even if they don’t necessarily want independence.

“Strategic separatists and their leaders have been using that ambiguity, that lower-bar threshold, to entice folks to vote not to leave, but rather to send Ottawa a message that Albertans need to be heard,” said Jared Wesley, a political science professor at the University of Alberta.

He told Al Jazeera that the message may be resonating with some voters.

Data collected by Viewpoint Alberta, a University of Alberta-based research initiative, suggests that two-thirds of voters who support the referendum say they’re doing so for strategic reasons, to send a message to Ottawa.

These are people Morgan calls “reluctant separatists”, people who are “at the end of their rope” and simply want Ottawa to pay attention.

title: ‘Anger and shame’: Macron denounces France’s nationwide rioting, looting
text:
French President Emmanuel Macron has expressed “anger and shame” over what he described as violent protesters’ attempts “to bring down the republic”.

In a televised address to the nation on Sunday, Macron promised that rioters and looters would “pay for their crimes”, after Saturday saw some of the worst urban violence in France in years.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Photos: Protests across France spiral into looting, blazes and clashes

list 2 of 3Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaotic

list 3 of 3Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?

end of list

The country’s Interior Ministry said that nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Saturday, with about 1,000 police and gendarmes injured.

Macron said there must be a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”.

The president pledged to launch a “crisis unit” to provide “urgent aid … for those who are going through difficult moments”. He added that “lessons will be learned” after the destructive violence erupted this weekend.

“We need to be clear: yesterday, our law enforcement officers and officials, despite their professionalism, were subjected to unprecedented violence in several cities,” he said.

“I’ve asked the government to provide all the lessons learned and to be able to anticipate it to make sure that this does not happen again,” Macron said, adding: “We need unity, we need calm and respect.”

Reporting from Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said Macron’s speech had “perhaps no surprises”.

“Whether it’s going to be enough to placate some people, I’m not really sure, because those who have been out protesting say they’re fed up of hearing these sorts of speeches by the French president,” Butler said.

The protests are quickly becoming a political football for parties vying for public support ahead of presidential elections next year.

Left-wing presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said the French government is “solely responsible” for the destruction during protests, and has “failed to organise the maintenance of public order”.

Far-right presidential hopeful Jordan Bardella called Macron’s Sunday speech “lamentable” and “cowardly”, saying the government has nothing left to offer the French people and “cannot even protect them”.

title: India’s crackdown on cockroaches, critics and cameras
text:
A wave of youth-led protests has returned to the streets of India’s capital, Delhi, after media reports revealed that the Electoral Commission removed about 130 million names from voter lists.

These protests differ from the unrest that exploded in July, though, by the attacks on the media.

Dozens of journalists and content creators have been detained, assaulted or blocked from doing their jobs. But tightening the screws on critical reporting doesn’t appear to be working, as a new generation rises to challenge the government.

Contributors:

Saba Naqvi – Author and journalist

Smita Sharma – Multimedia journalist

Shyam Meera Singh – Founder, Strike Originals

Sushant Singh – Lecturer, Yale University

On our radar

Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following protests calling for the release of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan.

The state’s response has followed a familiar pattern: A media blackout and internet shutdown, while casting protesters as rebels.

Reporter: Tariq Nafi

The rise of digital micro-Bolsonaros

It’s been more than three years since Jair Bolsonaro fell from power, yet the right-wing movement he started is still without a clear leader. Into that gap has stepped a new crop of young evangelical political influencers, who are tapping into a decades-old religious media machine to build their audience.

Their viral content ricochets across social feeds, mobilising followers and voters in ways old-school politicians just can’t match.

The Listening Post’s Nicholas Muirhead reports on Brazil’s evangelical influencers and the political space they are looking to take over.

title: How will Europe deal with youth-led protests?
text:
Weeks of student protests in France have grown into some of the worst unrest in Europe in recent years.

The demonstrations started as a call for reforms to the education system. But they have since expanded into protests against the high cost of living and planned cuts to social services.

And France is not alone. Demonstrators have taken to the streets in other parts of Europe. They are venting their frustrations against leaders they say have failed to address their needs, and putting pressure on their governments.

And right-wing parties are looking to seize the moment to make political gains.

title: Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
text:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the war with Russia “must be brought to an end” and that his country is preparing for the “next steps” of diplomacy to end the conflict.

The Ukrainian leader’s comments come amid a significant diplomatic fallout with US President Donald Trump, who on Friday night waived sanctions targeting Russia’s energy economy.

In a Sunday social media post, Zelenskyy wrote that he had a “conversation with the American president’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner”.

He added that “a lot depends” on the US position, but it’s clear there are “many things that matter to all of us”.

The Trump administration had already eased restrictions on Russian fuel imports on October 9, when it announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in an effort to tackle soaring fuel prices

The US Treasury temporarily authorised the imports despite existing sanctions, prompting criticism that the move could provide Moscow with revenue to sustain its war in Ukraine.

Trump has also criticised recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as “a disgrace”.

Nonetheless, Zelenskyy said his team is in “virtually nonstop communication” with their US counterparts and said a focus of dialogue is on the results of the talks in Florida and further steps.

US wavers on Ukraine’s access to tech

Zelenskyy also said he was “thankful” that the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a pause left the country particularly vulnerable to Russia’s regular ballistic missile attacks.

“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side,” Zelenskyy told NBC, adding: “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”

Kyiv has also reported restrictions on the speed of satellite service Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite connectivity network, provided to Ukraine by Musk’s company SpaceX.

Ukraine said its relays were experiencing a limit on how fast receivers could travel while maintaining connectivity, making it almost impossible to intercept Russia’s upgraded jet-powered long-range drones.

Musk had said any restrictions imposed on Starshield connectivity were the responsibility of the US government. The White House quickly rebuked that and in an NBC interview on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Zelenskyy “very reckless” for accusing the US of throttling connectivity.

title: GCC condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as Yemen fighting intensifies
text:
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has condemned repeated attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi fighters on Saudi Arabia and pledged support for the kingdom.

The political and economic bloc that includes Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates issued a statement on Sunday, shortly after their foreign ministers’ meeting in Manama, Bahrain.

The statement said an attack on any member affected all six, invoking a joint defence agreement and backing Saudi Arabia’s right to protect itself.

The condemnation came as the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis reported shooting down two drones near Riyadh and in Saudi Arabia‘s Eastern Province early on Sunday.

The coalition said another drone had been intercepted near the capital hours earlier, but did not identify who launched it.

Gulf ministers accused the Houthis of carrying out deadly strikes on civilian airports and vital facilities.

They also pressed for tighter enforcement of a United Nations arms embargo against the group and urged countries to formally designate it “a terrorist organisation”.

The ministers welcomed an October 15 statement from the UN Security Council (UNSC), the body responsible for maintaining international peace, which condemned Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and threats to Red Sea shipping.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government separately appealed to the UNSC to act against Houthi attacks on homes and state facilities.

In letters addressed to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the UNSC’s president for October, Aglaia Balta, the Yemeni government cited an attack on the presidential palace in Aden, where the government is temporarily based.

Separately on Sunday, UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan met Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud in Abu Dhabi to discuss regional security, the UAE’s state news agency WAM reported.

Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press offensives on several fronts.

The Yemeni military said the Houthis fired missiles towards the central city of Marib on Sunday, while government troops reported gains in Taiz, further south.

Government-aligned commanders said eight soldiers died in fighting in Lahij province on Saturday.

Government forces also claimed to have killed 12 Houthi fighters in southern Taiz, figures that could not be independently confirmed.

This latest phase of the war followed Houthi gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month.

Government forces launched a counteroffensive intended to recapture territory from the Houthis, who seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.

Civilians face deepening shortages

The fighting has uprooted more than 233,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration

title: 'Shouldn't have come if unwell': Minister defends public reprimand of Daler Mehndi
text: NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand minister Subodh Uniyal on Wednesday defended himself over reprimanding singer Daler Mehndi on stage during an event, saying the artiste should not have performed if he was unwell. Speaking to news agency PTI, Uniyal said Mehndi was only lip-syncing during the event and that, as a public representative associated with the event's organising committee, he came under pressure from people who wanted the issue to be questioned. "Daler Mehndi, being a big name, was invited to the Kunjapuri Fair. But during the performance, it became apparent that he was only lip-syncing and not singing. I, being a local representative and also associated with the organising committee, felt the pressure from people who wanted this to be questioned," Uniyal said. "Mehndi was not able to speak or walk. At that point, I thought he was under the influence of some substance. I don't know what, because a medical examination was not conducted," he added. Uniyal said he later learnt that Mehndi was unable to speak because he was unwell. "Being such a big artiste, he should have informed us about this. This fact was revealed only when he was interrupted. If he was unwell, he should not have come to perform," the minister said. "We were asked to make full payment of Rs 35 lakh in advance to the artiste; hotels were also booked in advance. I have nothing personal against Mehndi nor any intention to hurt him, but such a big artiste, knowing his condition, should have refused to perform," Uniyal said. "I stand by the fact that if an artiste's respect must stay intact, they should also work accordingly. I did not use any foul language while speaking to Mehndi," he added. The controversy erupted after Uniyal went on stage and expressed displeasure while Mehndi was performing at the Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair, a cultural event organised by the Uttarakhand government at Narendra Nagar in the New Tehri area on Sunday night.Congress demands minister's apology The controversy also took on political overtones, with Congress demanding that Uniyal publicly apologise for the way the episode was handled. “The treatment meted out to Mehndi is deeply unfortunate and runs counter to Uttarakhand’s glorious tradition of hospitality,” Amarjit Singh, general secretary of the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee, said.Artists rally behind Mehndi Meanwhile, several people from the entertainment industry, including actor Anupam Kher, stand-up comedian Vir Das and singers Shaan, Palash Sen, Gurdas Maan and Alisha Chinai, came out in support of Mehndi. They said the artiste, who has been singing for three decades, was unwell, did not drink and should have been treated with greater respect. "Couple of days ago, I saw a video in which Daler Mehndi ji was singing on stage and some minister got up and spoke to him insultingly. title: Trump's son 'opposed' Iran war, believed US should avoid another Middle East conflict
text:
Don Jr has not said anything publicly about his reported opposition

Donald Trump Jr, US President Donald Trump’s eldest son, privately opposed the war with Iran from its outset, reportedly believing Washington should stay out of another conflict in the Middle East. Trump Jr, who has long been sceptical of foreign military intervention, made his opposition known to his father, two people who spoke directly with him about the conflict told the Atlantic. He has not publicly broken with the president over the war. “Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can’t imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject,” a person close to Trump Jr told The Atlantic. Trump Jr’s reported opposition contrasts with the military campaign launched by his father alongside Israel against Tehran. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump Jr had backed his father’s promise to keep the US out of another Middle East war. “Remember when they said Trump would get us into a full-blown war with Iran?” he wrote on X in April 2024, as Iran launched a barrage of missiles and drones towards Israel. “Times like these should make us all realize how lucky we were to have Trump, his strength and his resolve,” he added. The Atlantic reported that Trump Jr’s opposition reflects his long-standing scepticism of foreign intervention. He was also particularly close to Charlie Kirk, the late conservative activist who had broken with the Trump administration to oppose the Iran war. “Don Jr. is the most MAGA of them all,” one of the people who discussed his opposition to the conflict told the publication.

MAGA divide over Iran war

The conflict has exposed divisions within the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement over the meaning of Trump’s “America First” agenda. The divide pits non-interventionists, who believe foreign wars divert resources from domestic priorities, against hawks who argue that the US should use its military power more aggressively against adversaries. Trump Jr’s reported position is part of a broader debate within the president’s political base over whether the war runs counter to the promises that helped Trump win the 2024 election. Doubts about the conflict have also emerged within the administration. Vice President JD Vance had reportedly voiced private opposition in the past during deliberations over whether the US should join Israel’s military campaign. CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were also sceptical of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s initial proposal in February for a regime-change operation, particularly one conducted through air strikes, according to The Atlantic. title: 'Remain vigilant, avoid crowds': India issues advisory amid France protests
text:
Protesters march during a demonstration in Marseille, southern France. France's government is unfurling massively ramped-up security measures for a fresh blast of marches and strikes against unpopular pension reforms.

NEW DELHI: The Indian embassy in France on Wednesday issued a safety advisory for Indian nationals living in or travelling to the country, urging them to remain vigilant amid ongoing protests, violent clashes and localised curfews. It asked citizens to avoid crowded places where demonstrations are taking place and follow instructions issued by French authorities. The embassy also advised Indians to monitor local news, check official government updates and stay informed about public transport disruptions. It shared emergency contact details for the Embassy of India in Paris and the Consulate General of India in Marseille. "In view of the recent developments and localised curfews imposed in France, please remain vigilant and exercise due caution. Please avoid large gatherings and crowded places where protests are taking place, and follow the instructions and advisories issued by the local French authorities," the embassy said in a statement on X. It also urged travellers to check updates on the French government's website and the Paris public transport operator RATP's website. Indian nationals can contact the Embassy of India in Paris at +33648340063 or email cons.paris@mea.gov.in in an emergency. They can also contact the Consulate General of India in Marseille at +33743162559 or email go.marseille@mea.gov.in.

France prepares for fresh demonstrations

The advisory comes as France prepares for another round of demonstrations scheduled for Saturday, October 24, following riots that caused widespread destruction and led to thousands of arrests on October 17, Xinhua news agency reported. French President Emmanuel Macron said on Wednesday that the government would use all available legal tools to prevent a recurrence of the violence. He was speaking to journalists during a visit to Qatar, according to French television channel BFM TV. Macron said declaring a state of emergency was not necessary at this stage, although the government could consider the measure later if required.

title: Rs 50k bond, no Jantar Mantar protests: What are the conditions of CJP leaders' release?
text:
NEW DELHI: A special executive magistrate on Wednesday ordered the release of Cockroach Janata Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, seven days after they were taken into custody. The CJP leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody on October 13 following a protest at Jantar Mantar seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the deletion of voters' names. CJP leaders Das and Ranka, along with 12 party members, allegedly trespassed into Jantar Mantar, which is no longer a designated protest venue, and obstructed police personnel on duty. The release order came hours after the two withdrew their petition in the Delhi high court challenging the extension of their custody.What are the conditions of release The CJP leaders were released after they gave written undertakings not to breach the peace and assured the court that they would not call for any protest at Jantar Mantar as long as it remains denotified as a protest site, Live Law reported. The leaders also assured the court that any protest they organise would be conducted within the four corners of the Constitution. Read more | Watch: 'Inquilab Zindabad', CJP leaders Saurav Das & Ashutosh Ranka come out of Tihar Jail In their undertakings, Ranka and Das expressed faith in the judiciary and its institutions, including the court of the special executive magistrate. The magistrate took the undertakings on record, Live Law reported.

After considering submissions from both sides and the written undertakings, the magistrate held that the immediate preventive measures under Section 135(3) of the BNSS could be secured by requiring the two leaders to execute bonds to maintain peace. Das and Ranka were also directed to furnish personal bonds and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each until the conclusion of the inquiry. The magistrate also directed them to appear before the court on every date of hearing and maintain peace and public tranquillity in accordance with the terms of their bonds and undertakings.

title: Monsoon's gone, El Nino isn't: Why India's weather worries are far from over
text: El Niño is putting the world on alert, and India could be among the countries facing its next major weather test. After a monsoon marked by a 13 per cent rainfall deficit, attention is shifting to whether the climate phenomenon will bring a warmer winter, disrupt rainfall patterns and add to the pressure on agriculture. From Indonesia’s raging wildfires to an unusually active Pacific hurricane season, its effects are already emerging across the globe. Now, the question is what a strengthening El Niño could mean for India in the months ahead. According to the BBC, El Niño has been strengthening for several months and is already influencing weather patterns worldwide, with Indonesia experiencing its worst wildfire season since 2015, heightened hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific and reduced monsoon rainfall in India. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has warned that the phenomenon could intensify further towards the end of 2026 and persist into 2027, raising concerns over its potential impact on temperatures, rainfall and extreme weather events across different regions. For India, the immediate concern is whether the strengthening El Niño will compound the effects of the deficient monsoon and influence winter temperatures, rainfall and agricultural conditions in the coming months.What is El Niño and how does it affect India's weather? El Niño is a climate phenomenon characterised by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate pattern that influences atmospheric circulation, wind systems and rainfall distribution across the world. For India, El Niño is closely watched because it is generally associated with a higher risk of below-normal southwest monsoon rainfall. The warming of Pacific waters alters atmospheric circulation and can weaken conditions that support the Indian monsoon, increasing the possibility of prolonged dry spells and rainfall shortages. While central India received near-normal rainfall, eastern and northeastern India recorded a 26 per cent deficit, classified as an exceptional drought, while southern states received 24 per cent less rainfall than average, according to the BBC. A strengthening El Niño could contribute to warmer-than-normal conditions in parts of India, potentially increasing pressure on water resources and agriculture. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), citing the South Asian Climate Outlook Forum, projected normal to above-normal maximum and minimum temperatures across much of South Asia during October–December 2026. Higher temperatures later in the winter could also threaten wheat yields if heat coincides with the grain-filling stage, although the impact will depend on actual weather conditions. title: Google’s order for thousands of Waymo taxis has left many in the US government worried
text:
Representative Image

​Google’s Waymo has ordered thousands of vehicles built in China. The Alphabet-owned robotaxi company plans to import electric vans made by Zeekr, a brand of China’s Geely Holding Group, as it expands its driverless taxi service across the US. Waymo is reportedly on track to import about 5,100 vehicles by the end of 2026, more than doubling a fleet that has largely relied on Jaguar I-Pace SUVs. ​ According to a New York Post report, the arrangement has worried US lawmakers and safety experts because the vehicles come from China while operating cameras, sensors, and autonomous systems on American roads. Waymo says the imported vehicles contain no Chinese connected-car technology and receive their software and sensors in Arizona. ​

Why lawmakers are concerned about Waymo’s vehicles

​ Waymo has renamed the Zeekr vehicle Ojai. The vans are already operating in Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Phoenix, and the company is expanding their use to additional cities. ​ The company says it imports only the physical vehicle and installs its American-developed autonomous-driving equipment at its Arizona facility. However, former National Highway Traffic Safety Administration adviser Missy Cummings said the vehicles would need inspection before they could independently verify their components. ​“I would have to get in and look at the physical construction of the car to know that that’s absolutely true,” Cummings said. “It’s very possible that the Chinese have layered in other sensors that are recording data and sending it back to China.” ​ Waymo rejected that concern, saying its vehicles undergo security testing and that it does not provide Zeekr with rider information, vehicle telemetry, source code, or data collected by its autonomous-driving system. ​

How the US government could affect Waymo’s expansion

​ US Commerce Department rules already restrict connected-vehicle software associated with China or Russia beginning with model-year 2027 vehicles. Restrictions on certain connected hardware are scheduled to apply from model year 2030. ​ Waymo says its arrangement complies with those rules because the Chinese-built vehicles arrive without the prohibited connected technology. A bipartisan proposal in Congress would close that opening by restricting vehicles manufactured in China, regardless of where their software and sensors are installed. Senators Bernie Moreno and Elissa Slotkin introduced the Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026. House China Select Committee Chairman John Moolenaar introduced companion legislation. ​ Moolenaar previously warned that “hidden malware could disable fleets of cars and trucks or turn them into battering rams on wheels.” ​ The bill would give Waymo three years to phase out affected Chinese-built vehicles, requiring compliance by 2030. Although it advanced through a Senate committee, broader consideration was delayed until after the November elections. ​

Trump said Ukraine needed a new president and later cliamed Putin appeared more interested in reaching a deal than Zelenskyy.

With US fuel prices soaring weeks before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump turned to a most unlikely supplier for relief. Russia. Moscow, which Washington has sanctioned for years over its war in Ukraine, is now being allowed to supply diesel to the US and global markets under a temporary licence issued by the Treasury Department. The decision came after a telephone conversation between Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin. The White House said the move will help bring down fuel costs for American farmers, truckers and families. But critics, including several Republicans, argue that the deal risks putting money into Moscow's hands while doing little to ease prices for American consumers. The timing is politically sensitive as Americans are preparing to elect a new Congress on November 3, and the cost of living remains a major concern. For Trump, the political calculation appears straightforward. If Russian supplies arrive quickly and in sufficient quantities, they could help ease fuel prices and give his party a political boost. If deliveries fall short or prices remain high, the administration could end up granting Moscow significant economic relief without delivering much for American consumers.

Trump has waved many sactions days before they were due to take effect under Graham Act.

How much difference can Russian diesel make?

Diesel prices averaged $6.28 a gallon on October 11, up 71% from a year earlier. The American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices, put the average at $6.33 on October 16. The impact extends well beyond motorists because diesel also powers the lorries that transport goods, tractors used by farmers and cargo vessels that move products around the world. When diesel becomes more expensive, the cost of transporting food and other essentials rises, eventually feeding into household bills. Farm-state Republicans had pressed the White House to act, with Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa and others calling for a ban on fuel exports to protect domestic supplies. Trump initially backed the idea, but the White House later ruled it out. The administration subsequently turned to Russian diesel. In announcing the deal, Trump said bringing down prices for American farmers, ranchers and truckers was his highest priority. Russian oil imports by different nations.

title: Missouri court overturns ruling giving couple ownership of neighbour's road
text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A Missouri couple who bought land without road access secured a legal route through their neighbour’s property, but a dispute over who would own that road led to an appeal. On August 26, 2026, the Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District, reversed a ruling that would have transferred ownership of the road to the couple, Clint Bowen and Morgan Bowen. According to the court’s opinion, published by Justia in Bowen v. Roeder, the couple qualified for a private road because their property had no public road access. However, the law entitled them to a permanent easement, not ownership of the land beneath the road.

Couple sought access to landlocked property

Bowen and his wife purchased a tract of landlocked real estate in St. Clair County, Missouri, in 2023, intending to build a family home there. Their property had no public road running through it or directly alongside it, leaving them without the necessary vehicle access. Dylan Roeder owned the adjoining tract immediately south of their land. A road on his property ran from the southeast corner of the couple’s property to a public road, making it a potential access route. The couple petitioned the circuit court to establish a private road under Missouri law, specifically Sections 228.340 to 228.358 of the Revised Statutes. Following a bench trial on August 21, 2024, the court found that their property lacked public road access and that the requested route was strictly necessary. On September 16, 2024, the court approved a private road 40 feet wide across part of Roeder’s existing road. The designated section measured approximately 428.24 feet long and covered about 0.39 acre, or 17,130 square feet.

Lower court changed its position on ownership

The circuit court initially ruled that the couple would own the land designated for the private road, while Roeder would retain certain rights to use it. Roeder challenged this decision, arguing that the couple should receive an easement allowing access rather than ownership of the underlying property. The court reconsidered the issue and, on October 25, 2024, amended its interlocutory judgment. It agreed that the statute was intended to provide access while limiting damage and inconvenience to the neighbouring landowner. The amended ruling therefore granted the couple a non-exclusive right of ingress and egress over the road. Court-appointed commissioners assessed the damages at $3,750 for the easement, pipe-rail fence and gate. The initial order also addressed responsibility for construction, maintenance and repairs, including the possibility of sharing those costs if Roeder retained rights to use the road. However, in its final judgment on March 10, 2025, the circuit court returned to its original position, awarding the couple fee-simple ownership of the designated strip while allowing Roeder to retain certain rights of use. title: Iyer's India face a test of adaptation in New Zealand
text:
Shreyas Iyer, Mitchell Santner

India, led by Shreyas Iyer, will look to extend their unbeaten run in T20I series in New Zealand as they begin a five-match rubber against the hosts on Thursday. The visitors, despite having limited time to rest, acclimatise and train after their arrival, will rely on their batting strength to take on the home side. India's most recent T20I series in New Zealand was in 2022. The match in Napier ended in a tie under the Duckworth-Lewis method after rain interrupted play. India went on to win the series, claiming victory in the only match that was not affected by rain. Only four batters in India's squad have played T20Is in New Zealand before — captain Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson and Shivam Dube. While Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma and 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi bring plenty of attacking options, they will need time to adjust to the pace and seam movement expected in local conditions. For Iyer, the series is an opportunity to prove himself on an overseas tour after his tenure as captain began with consecutive defeats in Ireland and England. Mitchell Santner's New Zealand side will look to put India under pressure. Iyer arrives after leading India to their second consecutive gold-winning campaign at the Asian Games and a hard-fought home series against the West Indies that ended in a draw. However, if the series follows the pattern of India's tour of the UK earlier this year, scrutiny of Iyer's leadership is likely to increase. He is expected to lead India at the T20 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand in two years. India will be without two key players in all-rounder Hardik Pandya, who is injured, and pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah, who will feature only in the ODI and Test legs of the tour. Pandya had led India during their 2022 tour of New Zealand.

title: Rafale Marine trials underway in Goa for INS Vikrant operations
text:
Indian Navy is conducting trials of the Rafale Marine fighter aircraft in Goa for modifications needed for INS Vikrant. These trials will ensure the aircraft can operate with the carrier's ski-jump launch and recovery systems. The Indian Navy has placed an order for 26 Rafale Marine aircraft, set for delivery by the end of 2028. Rafale M aircraft serves various missions, enhancing the Navy's combat capabilities.

Indian Navy is conducting trials of the Rafale Marine fighter aircraft in Goa to validate the modifications required for operating the French-origin aircraft from India's indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant, marking a key step towards strengthening the Navy's carrier-based combat capabilities. According to ANI, citing defence officials, the trials are focused on modifications needed to adapt the aircraft for operations from INS Vikrant. The Indian Navy has signed a contract for 26 Rafale Marine aircraft, with deliveries expected by the end of 2028 or early 2029. The trials are significant because INS Vikrant uses a Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery (STOBAR) system, in which aircraft take off using a ski-jump ramp and land by engaging arrestor wires on the flight deck. The Rafale M was originally designed to operate from CATOBAR (Catapult Assisted Take-Off But Arrested Recovery) aircraft carriers, which use catapults to launch aircraft. Integrating the French-origin fighter with INS Vikrant therefore requires validation of its compatibility with the carrier's ski-jump launch configuration, recovery systems and other onboard infrastructure. The trials will help establish the aircraft's suitability for operations from India's indigenous carrier.About Rafale Marine The Rafale Marine, also known as the Rafale M, is a carrier-based, twin-engine multirole fighter developed by French aerospace manufacturer Dassault Aviation for the French Navy. According to the French ministry of the armed forces, the aircraft is designed to operate from aircraft carriers and perform a range of missions, including air defence, air superiority, deep strikes, reconnaissance and anti-ship operations. It has maximum take-off weight of 24.5 tonnes and is powered by two Safran M88-E4 turbofan engines. It can reach the maximum speed of Mach 1.8, or approximately 2,200 kmph. The Rafale M features a naval-specific landing configuration and an arrestor hook to enable recovery aboard aircraft carriers. The fighter's avionics include the RBE2 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, which Dassault says can detect and track multiple aerial targets and detect and track naval targets. Its other systems include the Front Sector Optronics (FSO) sensor and the SPECTRA electronic warfare suite, designed to help detect, identify and respond to threats from enemy radars, missiles and lasers. title: US top court nixes Trump admin's bid to restrict medical care for transgender inmates
text:
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that the treatments raised security concerns and 'could no longer be justified.' A divided appeals court panel declined to lift the block, prompting the administration to approach the Supreme Court.

The US Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to let President Donald Trump’s administration immediately enforce restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates, leaving in place a lower-court order that allows treatments to continue while a legal challenge proceeds. The brief order did not explain the court’s reasoning. Conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented, saying they would have allowed the policy to take effect as the case moved through the lower courts. The policy followed an executive order by Trump, a Republican who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term. It directs the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care rules so that federal funds are not spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” Under the policy, prisons would halt gender-affirming surgeries, gradually withdraw hormone therapy and end social accommodations such as makeup and wigs. Mental health services would continue to be available. Transgender inmates challenged the restrictions in court. US District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered that their treatments continue. Lamberth, who was nominated by Republican President Ronald Reagan, noted that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects, including depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. The Trump administration appealed, arguing that the treatments raised security concerns and “could no longer be justified”. A divided appeals court panel declined to lift the block, prompting the administration to approach the Supreme Court. About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, according to court records cited by the Bureau of Prisons. Lawyers for the inmates argued that withdrawing treatment would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health. They also said the government had not presented evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates during the 30 years it had been provided. The Supreme Court has previously allowed other Trump administration policies affecting transgender people to take effect while legal challenges continued. These include restrictions on military service and passport sex markers. The conservative-majority court has also upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender minors and restricting transgender athletes from participating in women’s sports.

End of Article

From teen star to property owner

title: Man's $30 drawing later linked to Dürer, may be worth over $10m
text:
Photo credit: Agnews Gallery

A $30 estate-sale purchase in Massachusetts has turned into one of the most remarkable art discoveries of recent years. The small, unframed drawing, bought by an anonymous man in 2017, has been identified by leading scholars as an original work by German Renaissance master Albrecht Dürer. Now titled 'The Virgin and Child With a Flower on a Grassy Bench' and dated to 1503, the ink sketch is believed to be worth at least $10 million, with some estimates placing its value far higher. The news was reported by NPR, Smithsonian Magazine and Artnet News. Read more about it here:

A bargain no one expected

The buyer came across the drawing at an estate sale in Massachusetts, where it was displayed without a frame and priced at just $30. It showed a mother and child rendered in delicate ink on yellowed linen, and although it carried Dürer’s well-known “A.D.” monogram, neither the seller nor the buyer believed it was a genuine Renaissance work. The anonymous purchaser later said he bought it simply because he thought it was “a wonderfully rendered piece of old art,” as per the reports. He kept it at home, unaware that the modest sheet of paper might be an original drawing by one of the most important artists of the Northern Renaissance. The work had been sold by the daughters of the late architect Jean-Paul Carlhian. Their family had long assumed it was a modern reproduction, though its history appears to reach back to 19th-century French art collectors among the Carlhian ancestors.

From curiosity to masterpiece

According to Smithsonian Magazine, the turning point came in 2019, when art collector and Agnews Gallery shareholder Clifford Schorer heard rumours about the possible Dürer during a trip to Boston. After seeing the drawing, he described the moment as extraordinary, saying it was either the greatest forgery he had ever seen or a masterpiece. Experts then spent years examining the work. Their investigation focused on the materials, the monogram, the paper and the drawing’s relationship to Dürer’s known compositions. The verification process ultimately took about three years before scholars became confident that the sketch was authentic. Two details proved especially persuasive. First, Dürer had inscribed his initials using the same ink as the drawing itself, a practice seen on at least 20 other works made between 1501 and 1514. Second, paper conservator Jane McAusland identified a trident and ring watermark on the sheet, a motif found on more than 200 sheets known to have been used by the artist.

Scholars confirm the attribution

Leading Dürer specialists Christof Metzger, head curator at Vienna’s Albertina Museum, and Giulia Bartrum, formerly a curator at the British Museum, examined the drawing and judged it authentic, reports shared. Their assessment transformed what had been treated as an attractive old sketch into a newly recognised work by a Renaissance master. The drawing is now dated to 1503 and titled The Vi

title: Zuckerberg’s wife Priscilla Chan marks 10 years in Hawaii, donates $1.48m to hospital
text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have donated $1.48 million to Hawaii’s Wilcox Medical Center, the latest contribution in what Chan described as a 10-year philanthropic relationship with the island community of Kauaʻi. The donation was made via the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and will help fund a mobile MRI unit and a new 3D mammography machine at Wilcox Medical Center, according to Hawaii Pacific Health. The gift comes as Chan reflects on a decade of philanthropy in Kauaʻi. In a message published by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Chan said, “What began as a desire to give back to a place we call home has grown into lasting partnerships with organizations dedicated to strengthening communities, caring for local families, and stewarding the people and places that make Kauaʻi so special. According to the initiative, 2026 marks 10 years of philanthropic work on Kauaʻi, with more than $100 million committed to over 100 local organisations and more than $57 million invested directly on the island.

Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan funding healthcare infrastructure

Wilcox Medical Center said the $1.48 million donation will support two key imaging projects. The donation made by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan will pay for a MRI unit and a new 3D mammography machine. The mobile unit for MRI will work as a stopgap while the hospital renovates its existing MRI suite which is said to complete in coming eight months. For the uninitiated, Wilcox performs more than 4,000 MRI scans a year, and the temporary unit will keep those exams available during the work. The 3D mammography unit, along with the room renovations needed to install it, will support breast cancer screening. Wilcox says it was the first medical center on Kauaʻi to offer 3D mammograms, in 2010, and it performed more than 8,500 mammograms last year. The hospital notes that the clearer 3D images are especially valuable in Hawaiʻi, where many women have dense breast tissue. Wilcox CEO Jen Chahanovich said the couple has repeatedly stepped forward to make sure the community has access to the best medical technology.

More than $4 million donated to Wilcox by Chan Zuckerberg Initiative

According to Hawaii Pacific Health, the latest contribution is the couple’s second donation specifically aimed at expanding imaging technology at the hospital. Chan, a paediatrician, and Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, have now made five contributions to Wilcox programmes and services totalling more than $4 million. Previous donations have supported telemedicine initiatives, Covid-19 relief efforts, and renovations of the Wilcox Emergency Department and Trauma Center.

Health care the biggest focus

title: Part of Fred MacMurray's ranch bought for $21m now lists for $22m
text:
Part of Fred MacMurray’s sprawling 1,750-acre California ranch, the 52-acre Flax Estate and Vineyard is now listed for $22 million. (Photo: Facebook/DuMol.com)

A 52-acre estate in California’s wine country, once part of Hollywood actor Fred MacMurray’s sprawling ranch where he raised Scottish Black Angus cattle, has hit the market for $22 million. Located in Healdsburg’s Russian River Valley, the property includes 26 acres of organically farmed Pinot Noir vineyards, three residences and interiors by renowned designer Ken Fulk. According to Mansion Global, the asking price also includes the furnishings. Known as Flax Estate and Vineyard, the property is owned by philanthropists and restaurateurs Jeffrey and Laurie Ubben, who purchased it in 2016 for $21 million. The estate was originally formed from three parcels of MacMurray’s 1,750-acre ranch, which dates back to 1941.

Fred MacMurray’s former ranch has a Hollywood legacy

MacMurray, who enjoyed a career spanning five decades, appeared in more than 100 films. His credits include Billy Wilder’s 1944 classic Double Indemnity and popular Disney films such as The Shaggy Dog and The Absent-Minded Professor. He also played Steve Douglas, the father in the sitcom My Three Sons, which aired from 1960 to 1972. During his ownership of the sprawling ranch, MacMurray raised Scottish Black Angus cattle. Today, a portion of that historic property has evolved into a working vineyard estate that combines its Hollywood past with modern country living. “Rarely do we see a property with so much provenance,” said Alain-Martin Pierret of Compass Healdsburg, who co-listed the estate with colleague Haley Skerrett. He described it as a “pedigree boutique vineyard” and compared the grounds to a private Yosemite Park. The vineyard operation is reportedly ready to continue under new ownership. Buyers also have the option of hiring DuMOL, the winery co-owned by the Ubbens, to manage the vineyard.

Three homes, vineyard views and interiors by Ken Fulk

The estate comprises three residences: a renovated 1940s farmhouse, a contemporary home and a rebuilt caretaker’s cottage. It also has direct access to the Russian River and includes an entertainment barn. The approximately 4,000-square-foot contemporary home stands among mature oak trees and features a distinctive white geometric design. It has four bedrooms, four full bathrooms and one half bathroom. Expansive glass walls frame views of Mount St. Helena and Fitch Mountain. “It feels like a giant treehouse,” Pierret said, describing the home’s natural light, large windows and connection to the surrounding landscape. The 1940s farmhouse offers approximately six bedrooms and bathrooms, along with a range of recreational amenities. These include a 75-foot swimming pool, a spa, a gym, a sauna, tennis and bocce courts, orchards, and flower and vegetable gardens. “It has a porch, a gigantic dining room and a family room,” Pierret said. title: Sri Lanka’s dilemma: Iranian ships at its doorstep, US sanctions in the shadows
text:
Sri Lanka has announced it has no immediate plans to assist 19 Iranian oil tankers anchored in international waters off the island nation's coast, despite shortages of food, water and fuel aboard the vessels. “Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States,” a foreign ministry spokesperson told reporters in Colombo on October 9. The statement came in response to a Wall Street Journal report earlier this month alleging that US officials had “pressured” Sri Lanka to prevent local shipping firms from supplying the tankers with food and fresh water. However, the foreign ministry spokesperson said the US had not communicated any threat of sanctions if Sri Lanka stepped in to help. Nevertheless, the risk of sanctions appears to be shaping Colombo's response, whether or not Washington has issued a direct warning. Sri Lanka's dilemma is not simply about whether to assist the stranded Iranian vessels, but how far it can act independently when the prospect of US secondary sanctions looms over its decisions.

How Iranian ships became stranded near Sri Lanka, and Colombo’s dilemma

On February 28, the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran, triggering a war in the Middle East. Tehran retaliated with strikes against Israel and targeted American military bases across Gulf states. Iran also blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, a critical sea route, in March, prompting Washington to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports. The US blockade was later lifted before being reinstated in July. Its resumption left dozens of Iranian vessels stranded off Sri Lanka and neighbouring nations, unable to return home. It was against this backdrop that Sri Lanka said it would prioritise its national interests before assisting the Iranian ships. But where are the ships stranded, and is Colombo legally obliged to assist them? According to Sri Lankan foreign minister Vijitha Herath, around 47 foreign ships are currently anchored off the country's coast, 19 of which are Iranian-flagged. Herath said all the vessels are stranded within Sri Lanka's Exclusive Economic Zone but outside the 12-nautical-mile limit of its territorial waters. This creates a dilemma for Sri Lanka. Article 98 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) requires states to promote effective search-and-rescue services and ships to assist people in distress at sea. However, the extent of Colombo's legal obligation to provide supplies depends on whether the sailors are in distress and the circumstances of their requests for assistance, rather than simply the vessels' location outside territorial waters.

We haven’t provided them (Iranian vessels) with anything so far, and we don’t intend to do so in the future either. ... Such supplies to vessels are usually provided by the private sector, and this is a matter for them.

title: At 69, Delhi’s ‘stuntman’ continues Ramleela tradition of setting himself on fire
text:
Ram Prasad Tiwari is a 69-year-old performer who has been doing a dangerous stunt for nearly 50 years (Photo credit: Anuj Solanki)

BULANDSHAHR: At 69, Ram Prasad Tiwari, a stuntman, continues to perform a daring stunt during Ramleela events, setting himself on fire before jumping into a pool of water from a height of nearly 50 feet. Tiwari, a resident of Nand Nagri in northeast Delhi, performed the stunt at a Ramleela ground in Khurja area of Bulandshahr district. Speaking to TOI, he said he had been performing the dangerous act for nearly five decades. “I have been doing this stunt for almost 50 years,” Tiwari said, adding that he travels to different places to perform during the Ramleela season. For each day's performance, Tiwari receives Rs 8,000, which includes his travel expenses and accommodation. The work, however, is seasonal, and he has to find alternative means of earning a livelihood during the rest of the year. Tiwari said he sells clothes in local markets during the off-season to support his family. He has five children, three sons and two daughters, of whom two are married. His wife is a homemaker. Despite his age, Tiwari continues to undertake the high-risk performance, which draws attention during Ramleela celebrations. His act involves setting himself on fire and plunging into water from a height of around 50 feet.

title: Josh Allen’s unexpected reunion: Why did he recognize a whistle after 12 years?
text:
Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen reunited with former Reedley College coach Randy Whited before the game against the Las Vegas Raiders. (Image via Getty)

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen was heading toward the locker room before Sunday's game against the Las Vegas Raiders when a familiar whistle caught his attention. He turned toward the sideline and recognized a man he hadn't seen in 12 years: Randy Whited, his former junior college football coach. The reunion took place at Allegiant Stadium on Oct. 18, shortly before Buffalo's 33-30 victory. Whited had traveled to Las Vegas expecting to watch his former quarterback play. Instead, a friend's surprise arrangement brought him face-to-face with the player whose NFL future he had predicted back in 2014.

Who was the man who made Josh Allen turn around with a single whistle?

Whited coached Allen at Reedley College in California, where the quarterback spent the 2014 season before transferring to Wyoming. The two had not met in person since Allen's freshman year. According to Mike Maynard of the Buffalo Bills' official website, Whited traveled to Las Vegas with family and friends to see Allen play. He learned only a day before the game that someone had arranged a pregame meeting on the sideline. Whited initially hoped to catch Allen's attention and exchange a wave. The surprise meeting gave him considerably more than he had expected. As Allen finished warming up and walked toward the locker room, Whited used a sound he knew his former quarterback would recognize. "I just whistled, and I know he'd heard it before," Whited told Maynard. Allen immediately turned, spotted his former coach and jogged over to embrace him. The pair briefly caught up, with Whited congratulating Allen on his family before sending him back to prepare for the game. The moment carried additional meaning for Whited, who retired from coaching in 2016. He had followed Allen's career on television for years, watching his former junior college quarterback become one of the NFL's leading players. Whited also recalled an earlier encounter between Allen and his son at a Topgolf venue. Allen recognized his former coach's son and asked whether Whited was still spending time bass fishing. That interaction reinforced what Whited noticed during Sunday's reunion. Despite Allen's accomplishments, his former coach believed the quarterback still carried the same personality he remembered from Reedley. Allen's physical development was harder to miss. He stood 6-foot-3 and weighed 205 pounds during his junior college days. The Bills now list him at 6-foot-5 and 237 pounds. For Whited, seeing that difference in person after 12 years offered another reminder of how far Allen had progressed.

How did Randy Whited know Josh Allen would become an NFL quarterback before anyone drafted him?

Whited's confidence in Allen began during the 2014 season, long before the Buffalo Bills selected the quarterback with the No. 7 overall pick in the 2018 NFL

title: Joe Burrow’s ‘different side’ resurfaces as Ryan Clark defends Lane Johnson
text:
Joe Burrow reveals a different side of himself on The Pivot Podcast after Ryan Clark defends Lane Johnson’s mental health (Image via Getty: Joe Burrow)

Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is well-known for his confidence, ruthless competitive edge, and composed demeanor under immense pressure. However, the personality fans see on the gridiron may not tell his whole story. Burrow revealed another side of himself while speaking with former NFL safety Ryan Clark on The Pivot Podcast in 2024. Burrow’s revelation offered a glimpse into how his mindset changes as he prepares for an NFL game. This discussion has resurfaced online right after a broader conversation about NFL players’ mental health. Ryan Clark recently defended former Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Lane Johnson for choosing mental health over football. Clark even challenged longtime ESPN analyst Stephen A. Smith for his criticism on Johnson’s midseason retirement.

Joe Burrow reveals his different side on The Pivot Podcast

During the 2024 podcast conversation, Ryan Clark asked Joe Burrow why he did not have his parents, Jimmy and Robin Burrow, visit his house on the Saturday before a game. The Cincinnati Bengals quarterback explained that his mindset changes once the weekend reaches game preparation time. “That’s game time. That’s a different - once Saturday hits, that’s a different Joe [Burrow] now,” he said. Although he loves his parents and wants to be present with them, Burrow admitted that he can become difficult to be around as he prepares for a game. His focus shifts toward football, leaving him with limited time and energy to give to others, for that matter, even his parents. “And I don’t…like I love my parents and want to be present with them, but when it’s time to get ready for a game, I might not be the most pleasant person to be around, and I don’t have a lot of myself to give to anybody else,” he added. Burrow’s revelation highlights the personal discipline and razor-sharp mental focus required to play professional football. This commitment also shows that family relationships, even with those who brought you into this world, may quickly take a back seat when a player prepares for football - out of the sheer pressure of competition. While on one side, Joe Burrow gives up on his family for football with a firm football-focused mindset, the other side shows Lane Johnson choosing midseason football retirement after a 2-2 record for his mental health and family relationships. Ryan Clark cleverly identified both the players and put them forth before us through his Pivot Podcast. We know Burrow’s stance; now let’s check out Johnson’s story.

Ryan Clark defends Lane Johnson before Stephen A. Smith

Former Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Lane Johnson announced his retirement on October 6, 2026. He played 14 seasons for the Eagles and cited his mental health and family priorities as key contributors to his retirement.

title: Germany on alert for Russian sabotage after drone spotted near air base
text:
Germany has raised the threat of Russian sabotage against its military to the second-highest level for the first time, warning of a significant risk to its armed forces and military installations. According to German broadcaster WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the escalation follows the discovery of a drone carrying explosives near Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, which investigators suspect may have been intended to target military aircraft. The German defence ministry has confirmed the significant sabotage threat facing the Bundeswehr (German armed forces). The Bundeswehr's assessment warns that the threat is no longer limited to isolated military installations, raising concerns about further sabotage attempts in the near future. The warning comes amid a series of suspected drone surveillance incidents targeting sensitive military sites and infrastructure across Germany. The Wunstorf incident has emerged as a key concern for German security officials after a drone carrying explosives was discovered near the air base in September. Investigators suspect it may have been intended to target military aircraft, although the circumstances surrounding the drone and its intended use remain under investigation. The assessment also points to suspicious drone flights over the site of Germany's Arrow 3 missile defence system and other military facilities, as well as a camera discovered filming a strategically important railway station in Minden. These incidents have heightened concerns about surveillance of critical infrastructure and possible preparations for sabotage. German officials fear that such operations could go beyond intelligence gathering and surveillance to cause physical damage, disrupt military activities and threaten personnel. The suspected targeting of sensitive installations has raised concerns about the security of Germany's defence infrastructure as Berlin continues to support Ukraine against Russia's invasion. The Bundeswehr is responding by strengthening security at military installations, including through increased patrols, surveillance cameras and improved perimeter monitoring. The measures are aimed at detecting suspicious activity and protecting personnel and sensitive equipment against potential sabotage attempts.

End of Article

title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
text:
The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
text:
Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.
