title: 25,000 people to attend Ekta Divas parade in Gujarat: Union Home Secretary
text:
Around 25,000 people are likely to attend the Rashtriya Ekta Divas parade on October 31 at Ekta Nagar in Gujarat, Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan said on Wednesday (October 21, 2026). October 31 is celebrated to commemorate the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, India’s first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister.

The event is not an alternative to or a competition for the Republic Day parade, Mr. Mohan said. “Every event has its dignity, honour and place in the national perspective. Republic Day, which is to celebrate the coming to force of the Constitution, is sacred...It signifies an event which highlights the military capabilities of the country, it brings out the full might of the Indian armed forces on display. Ekta Divas is more to celebrate the achievements of the police forces, to showcase different elements, [and there is a] larger component of culture here. The perspective is slightly different. This year, we want to celebrate the end of Naxalism; the theme may be different next year. The core is the unity of the country. It’s not a competition to any other event,” Mr. Mohan said.

Ekta Nagar, where Sardar Patel’s Statue of Unity was inaugurated in 2018, is nestled between the Satpura and Vindhyachal mountain ranges in Gujarat.

Around 2,000 artistes from 126 Naxal-affected districts across the country will participate in this year’s Ekta Divas parade, cultural performances and other events. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend.

The theme of this year’s cultural events at the Rashtriya Ekta Divas celebrations is Vande Mataram. In the 150th year of the Vande Mataram, many newly introduced features during this year’s parade have been drawn from the Vande Mataram.

In another new feature of this year’s celebrations, the parade and all the performances would be held in the evening due to high temperatures during the day, Mr. Mohan said.

Usually, the tableaux were made and designed by either government Ministries and Departments or by the State governments or other government entities. This time, designs and features were determined for the tableaux through national competitions run on MyGov at the national level, and also in every district of Gujarat.

Weaving together all the themes and designs received from the national and State-level competitions, a total of 15 tableaux would be based on these designs, made entirely by the public, without any involvement of any government Ministry or Department. The government is moving towards the idea that the tableaux at important events would incorporate the aspirations of the common people rather than the structured themes of government entities and State governments, Mr. Mohan said, with a people’s tableau witnessed for the first time in Ekta Nagar.

Among the new initiatives aimed at highlighting the achievements of the security forces were eliminating Naxalism; showcasing the country’s cultural diversity; including a play on Anandamath written by Bankim Chandra

title: Vijayawada development top priority if elected Mayor, says A.B. Venkateswara Rao
text:
Former IPS officer A.B. Venkateswara Rao, who is contesting for the post of Mayor of Vijayawada Municipal Corporation (VMC) as an independent candidate with the support of the Congress, CPI, CPI-(M) and other parties, on Wednesday said comprehensive development of Vijayawada and finding effective solutions to the existing civic problems would be his priorities if elected as Mayor.

Addressing a press conference, Mr. Rao outlined his development agenda, promising 24-hour drinking water supply, improved sanitation, better roads, and measures to address property tax and traffic problems.

He said special attention would be given to the removal of encroachments along the Budameru, construction-related issues and flood prevention through planned infrastructure measures. He assured residents that funding would not be a constraint, as development works could be taken up using municipal revenues and funds allocated by the Centre.

Emphasising transparent administration, Mr. Rao promised measures to curb corruption, improve accountability among officials and ensure the proper utilisation of public funds. He also said small businesses and street vendors would be supported without being subjected to unnecessary hardships.

He expressed concern that shortcomings in the political and administrative systems were contributing to corruption and tensions among caste groups, adding that these issues needed comprehensive attention. Public health and safety would also receive priority, he said, outlining plans to control mosquitoes, address issues of open drainage, monitor canals and prevent water stagnation. He promised improved safety at schools, Anganwadi centres, small shops and small industries, along with greater transparency in issuing licences and granting permissions.

Mr. Rao proposed developing night bazaars, food courts and street markets to create employment opportunities for young people and provide better facilities for small traders. Developing parks, pedestrian pathways and other public infrastructure would be part of his vision to make Vijayawada a clean, green and safe city, he said.

AP Congress vice-president and Administrative In-charge Kolanukonda Shivaji said Vijayawada had witnessed significant development under Congress rule and pledged the party’s full support to Mr. Rao.

CPM district secretary D.V. Krishna also expressed support for the candidate, stating that his party had consistently worked for the city’s development and would back him as the INDIA alliance candidate.

title: Wires, contradictory statements of injured raise red flags in suspected IED blast
text:
The recovery of wires from the site of the explosion inside a flat on the fourth floor of an under-construction building on Jeremiah Road, and contradictory statements by the two injured in the blast, have raised red flags among investigators. An IED can be rigged by connecting an explosive to a trigger mechanism, using wires and circuit boards. The torch involved in the blast in this case is suspected to be the trigger.

Following the police questioning both the persons injured in the blast, Bengaluru City Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said, “They are giving contradictory statements.” “We are trying to reconstruct what happened and how the incident unfolded, based on their statements,” he added.

Police are trying to establish the antecedents of the two injured and have sought information about them from the police stations under whose jurisdiction their residences fall in their hometowns.

Another senior official said that the suspicious materials found at the scene are said to have been delivered there and were not originally present at the spot. Police are now analysing CCTV footage from the area and using other technical evidence to track down the source of this delivery.

Loud sound

The alleged blast occurred around 2.30 p.m. on Tuesday at the building on Jeremiah Road, a quiet residential lane within the Pulakeshinagar police station limits.

Speaking to presspersons, Mansur, a resident of the locality, said neighbours had initially suspected a cylinder blast but later learnt that a “battery” had exploded.

“The sound of the blast was very loud, and all the surrounding buildings also heard it. When the residents went there, one of the injured person’s fingers was hanging from the hand, and he was subsequently taken to the hospital,” he said.

The under-construction building is situated among several residential houses in an area comprising both homes and commercial establishments.

Mr. Singh said some flats in the building where the blast occurred had been completed and were occupied, while interior work was under way in others. The blast occurred in a house where interior work was in progress.

Police informed late

The police were not informed of the blast right away, sources said. The injured were taken to Bowring and Lady Curzon Hospital, where doctors filed a Medico Legal Case (MLC) and intimated the jurisdictional police.

According to Mr. Singh, the police received the Medico-Legal Case (MLC) report in the evening, following which the city police’s Anti-Terrorism Squad and the Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) rushed to the location and examined the scene.

HM advises caution

Karnataka Home Minister Priyank Kharge said that it was not yet clear whether a chemical reaction had triggered the blast or whether it was caused by an IED. “This can be ascertained only after the FSL report is out,” he said, urging people not to believe rumours.

title: Heavy rain in Tirupati as low pressure area forms off Tamil Nadu coast
text:
Tirupati district received heavy rain in the 24 hours ending 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, with Tada recording 109.8 mm, Satyavedu 85.4 mm and Tirupati Aero 76.4 mm, according to the Meteorological Centre in Amaravati. The district’s average of 49.5 mm was more than eight times its normal for the day.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said a low-pressure area formed over the southwest Bay of Bengal off the Tamil Nadu coast at 5.30 a.m.

According to the Amaravati centre, thunderstorms with lightning are likely at isolated places in Prakasam, Nellore and parts of Rayalaseema on Thursday, and in most northern coastal districts, Prakasam, Nellore and most Rayalaseema districts on Friday. Strong winds of 30 to 40 kmph, gusting to 50 kmph, are likely at isolated places across the State until Saturday morning. The centre forecasts isolated light to moderate rain through October 27, becoming scattered in the coastal districts on that day.

In an update based on 5.30 p.m. observations, the Cyclone Warning Centre (CWC), Visakhapatnam, said the upper air circulation over the Gulf of Thailand had emerged into the north Andaman Sea. It is “very likely” to move west-northwestwards, and another low-pressure area is likely to form over the southeast and adjoining east-central Bay of Bengal around October 23. The low is then likely to move northwestwards and intensify further.

P.L.N. Murthy, Head of the CWC, said Visakhapatnam would “definitely” receive rain around October 27, possibly from the evening of October 26.

Prakhar Jain, Managing Director, Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA), said that the low-pressure area could form by Friday and that heavy rain was likely in coastal Andhra Pradesh next week. He advised fishermen not to venture into the sea from Sunday and those already at sea to return before then.

According to the Amaravati centre, the State received 47.3 mm of rain from October 1 to 21 against a normal of 111.7 mm, a deficit of 58 per cent. Only Tirupati, Chittoor and Annamayya districts received more than their normal rainfall.

title: Cargo vessel sinks off Beypore coast; all eight crew members rescued
text:
A cargo vessel carrying about 160 tonnes of construction materials and other goods sank nearly 18 nautical miles off the Beypore coast late on Tuesday night. All eight crew members on board were rescued by the Indian Coast Guard and brought ashore by Wednesday (October 21) morning.

The vessel, MSV Jesus Heart, was on its way from Beypore to Kavaratti in Lakshadweep when the accident occurred around 11.25 p.m. on Tuesday (October 20).

The Coast Guard launched a rescue operation soon after receiving an alert. A tugboat was used to rescue the eight crew members, who were safely brought to shore by Wednesday morning.

Officials from the Beypore Port said it was the timely intervention of the Coast Guard that averted a major tragedy. They said they were awaiting further details regarding the circumstances that led to the sinking.

title: Rubio meets Adani, Chandrasekaran; visits Reliance’s Jamnagar refinery
text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani and Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran in Mumbai on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) before heading to Jamnagar in Gujarat to visit Reliance Industries’ oil-refining complex.

Mr. Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai on Tuesday afternoon (October 20), first met Mr. Adani, followed by a meeting with Mr. Chandrasekaran, sources said.

Neither side released details of the meetings.

The visit comes as India and the U.S. seek to deepen commercial and strategic ties, with energy security, manufacturing and technology among the areas of potential cooperation.

Mr. Rubio’s Jamnagar visit puts energy and industrial investment at the centre of his India trip, with the Reliance complex emerging as a focal point for potential cooperation between Washington and New Delhi on global oil supplies.

The refinery’s ability to process a wide range of crude grades makes it strategically significant as the U.S. explores expanding markets for Venezuelan oil and India seeks to diversify its energy supplies.

Mr. Rubio has said Washington is in discussions with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude as production in the South American country rises.

Mr. Rubio, accompanied by his wife, Jeanette Dousdebes Rubio, toured the world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex, the Vantara wildlife rescue and conservation centre, and Reliance’s emerging clean-energy manufacturing hub, people familiar with the visit said. He spent a few hours in Jamnagar before departing for the United States. Almost the entire Ambani family, led by billionaire Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani, welcomed the U.S. delegation. Those present included his wife, Nita Ambani, daughter Isha Ambani and her husband, Anand Piramal, and younger son Anant Ambani and his wife, Radhika Merchant, along with Reliance Industries Executive Director P.M.S. Prasad and U.S Ambassador to India Sergio Gor. Mr. Gor said liquefied petroleum gas from the U.S. had risen sharply as a share of India’s imports. “Over the past year, India’s imports of US LPG have surged from under 10 per cent to 67 per cent, making the United States India’s largest LPG supplier,” he said in a post on X. He also highlighted Reliance's planned investment in a new refinery in Texas as an opportunity to expand U.S. energy production and create jobs.

title: Congress leaders in the dock for displaying palapitta during Dasara festivities
text:
Controversy erupted around Congress party leaders using caged birds during a public event on the occasion of Dasara festivities, here on Wednesday.

In a social media post, chief of the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee B. Mahesh Kumar Goud could be seen holding a palapitta or Indian Roller Bird brought to him in a cage, showing it to the audience, and then releasing it, while announcements blared from the megaphone, that the palapitta had arrived.

Witnessing the roller bird on the occasion of Dasara is considered auspicious in Telangana, giving rise to the practice of illegal capture of the bird for a quick buck.

Among the local Congress leaders surrounding him is former corporator from Uppal of the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation’s Rajitha Parameshwar Reddy, along with her husband M. Parameshwar Reddy, who is said to have organised the festivities in Uppal Municipal Stadium.

Mr.Parameshwar Reddy posted pictures of the same on his X account, owning up the celebrations, attended by a large number of people.

Forest officials were alerted about the incident by a post from the account with the user name ‘Forests And Wildlife Protection Society-FAWPS’.

‘We urge the non working forest dept of Telangana to thoroughly investigate and take immediate and strict action against this,” the post said, while featuring the video clip.

Medchal Malkajgiri district forest officials informed that a case has been registered under the relevant sections of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 against those responsible, including Mr.Parameshwar Reddy.

title: Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
text:
Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said.

Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and his European allies have been pressing Moscow for an immediate resumption of the talks suspended in February, and Ushakov said a new round could be held next month.

Russia has for months refused talks as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks.

Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Monday.

It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after talks in Oslo that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.

Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".

Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.

Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."

A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine".

"This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".

Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

The talks in Oslo and St Petersburg - which Witkoff described as "constructive" - were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.

Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

He was heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".

title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
text:
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.

Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.

Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".

It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.

Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.

Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.

Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.

The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.

Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders...

"We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."

On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".

He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.

Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.

"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."

"Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.

Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.

The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October

title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
text:
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.

Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".

The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.

Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.

"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."

He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.

"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.

Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.

He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.

In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.

The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.

Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.

"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."

Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.

Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.

Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional

title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
text:
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.

While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.

US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.

Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.

The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.

He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield".

A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".

Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued at around $1tn.

While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.

SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June.

title: Pakistan arrests man wanted by US over $126m postage fraud case
text:
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

title: Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
text:
The Gambia will use funds received from the US from the forfeiture of long-time ruler Yahya Jammeh's property to pay victims of his rule, authorities have said.

The Gambia's Reparations Commission said it received $2.5m (£1.86m) from the sale of a mansion in Maryland owned by former leader of the West African nation.

The US had in 2022 secured the right to sell the property on grounds that it was acquired through "criminal proceeds and misappropriated Gambian public funds".

Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years after taking over in a coup in 1994 - a time marked by allegations of human rights abuses forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.

On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.

It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".

Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.

He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.

Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.

In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.

A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.

There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.

Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.

A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

title: Family of prison officer killed by IRA receives state apology
text:
The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.

Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.

Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.

There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing.

The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the Dáil (Irish parliament).

Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology.

Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.

The Stack brothers left the Dáil (lower house of Irish parliament) chamber when Sinn Féin TDs spoke during the State apology.

Speaking outside Leinster House after the State apology, Austin Stack called on Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald to "address our concerns" around their father's murder.

"The IRA were responsible for the murder my father. The leader of the opposition has consistently said that the IRA campaign was justified," he said.

"The leader of the opposition did not dignify and respect my family by coming into the chamber today and because of that, we took the action that we did, in withdrawing from the chamber when Sinn Féin representatives were speaking."

Speaking to reporters in Belfast, where she was being interviewed by the Police Service of Northern Ireland in relation to protests at Garvaghy Road, McDonald welcomed the State apology.

"I can only imagine the trauma that they have been through for a long time," she said.

"The IRA has acknowledged responsibility and expressed sorrow for the death of Brian Stack, has said that it shouldn't have happened and I think they made those statements very clearly more than a decade ago and I think that was the right and the correct thing to do."

In a further statement, a Sinn Féin spokesperson said a number of senior party TDs made contributions in the Dáil, and that it was regrettable that McDonald was unable to attend due to her scheduled police interview.

"Our thoughts are with Sheila Stack and her sons. Brian Stack's killing was wrong and should never have happened. We are deeply sorry for their loss and suffering.

"Sinn Féin acknowledges the hurt caused by republican actions in the past. We welcome the Irish government's apology for the investigative failures that compounded the family's pain. They deserve truth and justice.

"Our position is clear: Investigating Brian Stack's killing is the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. We support that work and the family's right to answers."

title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case linked to East Africa
text:
Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state.

Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests.

The patient, who health sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian and is the wife of a diplomat, is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.

She developed symptoms on Wednesday 7 October, four days after arriving in the country, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified.

Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014.

Uganda's Ministry of Health has stressed there are currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country.

"We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," it said.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.

It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.

Following the latest case in Nigeria, Uganda's health ministry said preliminary information indicated that the patient had transited through Uganda without symptoms.

In a statement on X, Uganda's Director General of Health Services Charles Olaro said the woman had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.

He said her symptoms had only developed after arriving in Nigeria.

The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.

The woman's exact travel history - key to tracing contacts - appears to be unclear at the moment.

"The location of exposure remains under investigation. The government of Nigeria is yet to provide detailed information on her travel itinerary and clinical history which will guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing," Olaro said.

title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
text:
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.

A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.

The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.

South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.

Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.

The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.

"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday, external.

The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.

Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.

The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state.

A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said.

Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said.

Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known.

Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them.

The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time

title: Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
text:
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.

Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"

But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?

The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?

Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.

Just listen to the way they talk about each other.

"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.

The verbal assault has continued this week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.

Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".

"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."

For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.

But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."

Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.

"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.

But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?

In some ways, we've been here before.

After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.

The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.

One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.

title: Alberta's decisive decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
text:
"Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.

It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.

But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.

Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.

Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.

Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."

Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too.

"Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.

Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".

Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.

The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls.

"I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."

For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.

In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.

He didn't have to.

And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.

But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast.

"Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding dire

title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
text:
A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.

Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.

Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.

Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.

She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.

Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.

She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".

"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.

Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.

"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."

Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.

Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
text:
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.

Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.

title: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
text:
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.

Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.

The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.

For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.

In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.

This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.

He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.

Yet the photographs tell a different story.

Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.

While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.

There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.

China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened.

South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.

The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.

In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.

So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.

North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.

Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.

Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader.

title: Tourist found guilty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
text:
A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.

Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.

Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.

Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.

A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".

"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.

"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.

Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.

He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.

The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.

During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.

It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.

Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.

A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
text:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.

The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.

The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.

Marseille mayor Benoît Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.

Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.

Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The Préfecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".

A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.

French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.

Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".

Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.

He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.

Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.

Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".

On Tuesday, Mélenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".

title: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
text:
The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.

Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre.

"They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.

His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.

He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder.

Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings.

"When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child.

Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."

The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".

"I left school when I was seven," says Dan.

Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.

He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life".

"I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.

title: Cornell Jane Doe says embattled university head doubted her gang-rape allegation
text:
A former Cornell student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has said she felt "unsupported and disbelieved" by the university president.

Known anonymously as Jane Doe, she has written a letter accusing President Michael Kotlikoff of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.

The Ivy League institution in upstate New York says her account of the Cornell head's reaction is "incorrect".

She addressed her letter to campus faculty who will hold a rare vote this month on Kotlikoff's leadership. Doe filed her lawsuit last month alleging she was raped by several men in October 2024 at a Chi Phi fraternity party.

All seven former fraternity members accused by Doe have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.

Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police, and the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but the case has since reopened.

Responding to Doe's initial allegation, Cornell said it had opened an internal investigation, as well as a civil rights inquiry.

In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received "a second-hand account" of Kotlikoff's reaction and that his "initial response" was "along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'"

Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on 8 November, about three weeks after the fraternity party.

She noted that Kotlikoff had a conversation with the then-president of her sorority and that other staff members were present, at least one of whom "appeared distressed" by the college president's question.

Doe said in her letter: "It diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."

She said she wrote the letter so that faculty "can make an informed choice" ahead of their 28 October vote on whether to express no confidence in Kotlikoff's leadership.

The university confirmed receipt of the letter from Doe's lawyer.

But in a statement to the BBC, a Cornell spokesperson said: "The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account."

The spokesperson said Kotlikoff's question about the delay in reporting the alleged rape "was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024".

"He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting," the spokesperson said.

title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
text:
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.

If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.

The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.

"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.

There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.

Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.

The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.

It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.

Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon.

"The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained.

"But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."

The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.

Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.

This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.

The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g.

"It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.

"However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said.

Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.

There are two competing ideas.

Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.

Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity.

"When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell.

"It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out real

title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
text:
Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.

The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence.

"The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".

A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.

The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."

In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.

A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.

Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.

Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range.

"The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested.

"In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said.

"Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.

Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.

Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.

"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."

The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.

title: Macron makes surprise Saudi visit as France secures extra diesel supplies
text:
French President Emmanuel Macron visited Riyadh on a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in Saudi Arabia since the Houthis intensified their attacks this month.

The unannounced trip comes as Saudi Arabia agreed to supply extra diesel to France “for as many months as necessary”, the Elysee Palace told the AFP news agency on Wednesday.

list 2 of 3What are Italy’s new measures against violent protests?

list 3 of 3Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?

end of list

The visit aims to “demonstrate France’s solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies”, the French presidency said earlier.

The diplomatic push follows days of rioting in France, fuelled by the cost of living, especially as the US-Iran war and Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy prices high.

Faced with criticism of his Gulf tour at home, Macron told reporters he was just “doing his job” in a bid to “ease tensions” over petrol prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France.

“There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.”

Macron met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Saudi capital, and the two agreed to consult on expanding security cooperation and on infrastructure projects to bypass the blockaded strait, the palace said.

It did not say how much extra diesel Saudi Arabia would supply.

Macron’s Gulf tour

The deal follows pledges secured earlier in Macron’s Gulf tour. The presidency said on Tuesday that the United Arab Emirates had committed to about 100,000 tonnes a month, with a further 100,000 tonnes monthly to be secured in Bahrain.

Together with Saudi deliveries, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just more than 10 percent of its consumption, it said.

Meanwhile, France is also sending military assets to Saudi Arabia, under an earlier agreement, to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

The United Kingdom also announced on Tuesday that it would deploy fighter jets to help shield the kingdom. Both countries say their support is purely defensive.

Analysts say the moves protect Saudi oil exports that matter to Europe’s energy markets and bolster the Gulf alliance as the US shows reluctance to offer direct military help. They also carry risks, analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

title: Paris shopkeepers fear more destruction after riots destroy livelihoods
text: ‘I have nothing left.’ Small business owners in Paris say they are traumatised after rioters looted their shops. With more protests expected across France on Saturday, Al Jazeera’s Virginia Pietromarchi speaks to shopkeepers fearing further destruction.

title: Canada wants to expand its LNG business. Critics raise red flags
text:
Kitimat, British Columbia: As Canada tries to position itself as an emerging leader in global liquefied natural gas (LNG) markets, it risks locking in multidecade, multibillion-dollar contracts with companies whose current and past ventures include human rights abuses and environmental damage.

LNG Canada, which began operations in mid-2025 in Kitimat in British Columbia on the country's west coast, is the nation's first major export facility.

In late September, it gave the green light to a $33bn expansion which will double production in the coming years at Kitimat.

But the Kitimat plant has had challenges with its flaring equipment since beginning commissioning in late 2024. In 2025, the new liquefaction facility burned 350 million cubic metres of gas due to an issue with its main flare stack.

“The flaring noise was on a whole other level when they were first getting started up,” a resident who asked not to be named said in an interview. “It was just huge, way bigger than I think it was supposed to be.”

“I am devastated about the changes to my home territory,” another resident said. “I can't always see the stars like I used to from my parents' place here. My friend returned temporarily, and her asthma has been much worse.”

The residents requested to remain unnamed because Kitimat is a small community and the industrial project is a major employer and donor to local organisations.

The project has political support, especially as Canada faces economic pressures from United States President Donald Trump’s administration, which has unleashed a slew of tariffs on it, including on Canadian steel, lumber and aluminium in 2025 and added an additional suite of tariffs on Canadian products worth $20bn in August, including wine, dairy and textiles.

Since Trump started his tariff campaign, the Canadian government has announced a flurry of deals and agreements aimed at diversifying trade partners and expanding domestic infrastructure developments.

‘It’s all about investment’

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government recently added two LNG developments – LNG Canada and Ksi Lisims LNG – to its major projects list, promising strong federal support. The Major Projects Office, a dedicated agency, has been established to speed up infrastructure projects deemed to be of national interest.

“Canada is building big again,” Carney said at a news conference in Vancouver following the announcement. “A year ago, the federal government referred LNG Canada Phase 2 to our Major Projects Office. One office. One point of contact. One goal: get to the right decision, rapidly and efficiently. Working with Shell and LNG Canada, British Columbia and First Nations, we have accomplished exactly that.”

title: Catalonia’s new far right: How anti-Muslim sentiment is reshaping politics
text:
Barcelona, Spain – Almost a decade after a failed independence bid in Catalonia, anti-migration and anti-Muslim sentiment has replaced secession as the driving force among voters in this wealthy region.

A new far-right party, Alianca Catalana, or Catalan Alliance (AC), which wants a crackdown on migration and has targeted Islam as a threat to society, has surged in the polls in a region with the largest Muslim population in Spain.

The party is on course to become the second biggest political force in Catalonia after the Socialists at the next Catalan regional election in 2028, polls predict.

It has capitalised on the anti-migrant sentiment sweeping Europe, which has seen victories for the far-right in Germany, Italy, and France.

The rise of Catalan Alliance has alarmed Muslims, who fear a backlash in a country which has previously seemed welcoming.

“This has surprised all of us,” said Soukayna El Abdi, president of the Young Moroccans of Ripoll, referring to the party’s growth.

“Most people come to integrate, to work and live among others. The rise of [Catalan] Alliance is about unfounded hate. They spread lots of things about our community which are not true.”

Spain will vote in a snap election in November. Polls show the conservative People’s Party and the far-right Vox gaining support. The rise of the Catalan Alliance shows a shift towards the right in the fourth biggest economy in the eurozone.

The party backs independence and has taken support from the other secessionist parties, Together for Catalonia and Catalan Republican Left, which were behind the failed bid to break away from Spain in 2017.

“All my friends support Catalan Alliance. There are too many migrants around now and Islam is a threat,” Eduard Lopez, a businessman from Molins de Rei near Barcelona, told Al Jazeera. “These other independence parties are from the past. They failed to do what they said they would.”

Silvia Orriols, leader of Catalan Alliance, is also mayor of the town.
