title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
text:
Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopef

title: Brazil’s election and the battle for the Amazon – podcast
text:
For the Amazon and the communities who live there, the stakes in Sunday’s Brazilian presidential election runoff could scarcely be higher.

Our Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips heads to Roraima, the country’s most northern state, to hear from voters, preachers and politicians in a region that heavily backed Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round.

He finds them all hopeful that the far-right candidate will bring back the mining that his father Jair so heartily encouraged when in power in an administration that oversaw the felling of 11m acres (4.5m hectares) of rainforest.

Tom also meets Indigenous activists determined to fight back even if the Bolsonaros take power again.

title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
text:
When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).

“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.

But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.

This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.

While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.

“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”

The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.

The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.

The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.

Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”

Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agr

title: North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South
text:
Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.

The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.

Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music ​and news criticising Pyongyang.

If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.

At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.

The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.

Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.

Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.

The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.

On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.

The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.

Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.

North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

title: Mother sought advice from Alan Jones after broadcaster’s alleged indecent assault of her son, court hears
text:
The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones continued to seek advice from the broadcaster after the teenager was allegedly indecently assaulted at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm, a Sydney court has heard.

The divorced mother told the Downing Centre court she had developed a pattern of not trusting herself and she continued her correspondence with Jones because: “I knew he knew about everything; he had an opinion about everything.

“I was in a web of dependency with Mr Jones,” the witness said on her last day in the witness box on Friday.

She previously said she corresponded with Jones after he allegedly kissed the 17-year-old and put his tongue inside his mouth out of fear Jones would withdraw his financial support.

During cross examination, defence barrister Claire O’Neill suggested the mother continued to correspond with Jones not because she was scared but because she wanted more money out of him.

O’Neill asked: “You did not continue to communicate with Mr Jones because you were scared of his influence over your finances, did you?”

The witness replied: “I absolutely was.”

Her son, complainant A, is one of five men who allege Jones, 85, sexually touched or indecently assaulted them between 2003 and 2020. All five have now completed their evidence.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.

Under cross-examination by the defence, the witness agreed she wrote to Jones about her son’s late university application, a superannuation payment, outstanding legal fees and attaining a Sydney Cricket Ground membership for her son.

She was shown an email in which she provided Jones with an update on her son’s university application. The defence asked: “You wanted to lay the groundwork for having Mr Jones pay the [legal] bill?”

The mother said the suggestion was “absolute rubbish” and she was “proud of him” for finishing year 12 under difficult circumstances and wanted to convey that in the email.

She agreed she sent Jones information about the cost of repairs to her Land Rover but denied she was asking him to pay the bill.

“You have told lies in this court about why you continued to have contact with Jones?” O’Neill asked.

The witness replied: “Absolutely disagree, that’s rubbish.”

O’Neill: “You were taking advantage of Mr Jones’s generosity for as long as you could?”

Witness: “Absolute rubbish.”

When she was asked why she shared personal information with Jones about the deterioration of her relationship with her son she became emotional.

“My son, who was a child, suffered trauma and didn’t share it with anyone and it had an effect on his relationship with me and a lot of other people.”

Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright what that trauma was, she replied: “I was referring to what happened to him at Fitzroy Falls”.

The trial continues.

title: ‘I’ve killed people’: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to friend and asked for help cleaning ‘mess’, court told
text:
Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to killing two men, telling his friend it was an “out-of-body experience”, before attempting to play it off as a joke, a court has been told.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Lamarre-Condon’s friend, whose identity is suppressed, told the New South Wales supreme court on Friday that the officer arrived at his workplace the day Baird and Davies were killed.

Lamarre-Condon told him “I’ve done something”, and when the friend asked for an explanation, the policeman said “I’ve killed people”, the jury was told.

“I said ‘are you fucking kidding me?’, he said ‘I wish I was’,” the friend told the court. “He said it just felt like an out-of-body experience and it just wasn’t him.”

The friend said when he asked how Lamarre-Condon did it, the officer said with a gun.

He then made a gesture with his fingers indicating a firearm and said “pew pew”, the friend told the court.

When asked for more details, Lamarre-Condon allegedly said: “I shot the first one through the head and the second one through the door.”

Lamarre-Condon then said the second person wasn’t meant to be shot but he “couldn’t leave any witnesses”, the friend told the jury.

The officer asked his friend to leave work to help “clean up his mess”, noting the bodies were heavy and he needed to buy a new door.

The friend then returned to his workplace and explained the situation to his team lead, who told him to tell Lamarre-Condon he had a meeting he couldn’t miss.

Lamarre-Condon later messaged the friend and asked “I should get an Oscar, hey?” before going on video call and saying “got you”.

The friend then got upset, saying, “it’s not a fucking joke, you’re mentally fucking with me”, the court was told.

The policeman responded: “OK it is real but I just didn’t want you to tell anyone.”

The friend told the jury that on 20 February 2024, the day after the alleged murders, the pair went to dinner and Lamarre-Condon said he needed to “throw out bloody clothes and things”.

He then made a gesture to indicate his legs were sore and said: “I didn’t realise bodies would be heavy.”

Shortly before Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to police, the friend contacted a lawyer who attempted to connect him with NSW police.

But police said: “Is it worth our time coming out? It’s really busy,” the court heard.

The lawyer responded: “You’ll want this information.”

Earlier on Friday, the friend revealed he had travelled overseas in late 2023 for a trip with Lamarre-Condon.

He said that while overseas, Lamarre-Condon told the friend: “I need to find a spot … to purchase a silencer.”

The officer explained he was going hunting on a mate’s farm, the jury was told.

title: Embattled Queensland minister Amanda Camm quits Crisafulli frontbench citing health and safety reasons
text:
The Queensland minister Amanda Camm has resigned from cabinet following months of pressure over the state government’s handling of the child safety system and efforts to prevent domestic and family violence.

Camm told reporters on Friday the decision to step down was “mine alone”.

She suggested that some criticism of her had gone beyond “public scrutiny and accountability” and cited the recent alleged attack on federal MP Helen Haines.

Over the past year she had experienced harassment, threats, bullying and vilification, she said.

Camm had recently taken six weeks of medical leave, including undergoing a surgical procedure. She said she had realised her recovery would be “ongoing” and that she would not be able to continue perform her ministerial duties, given the workload and “the ongoing stresses”.

“It would be unfair to the government for me to take further leave,” Camm said.

A replacement is expected to be announced later on Friday.

Before taking leave, Camm had been the government’s most under-pressure minister. Her relationship with Tim Mander, the sport and Olympics minister, had placed both under scrutiny in parliament and the press.

But it was her dual responsibilities – child safety and the prevention of family violence – that had heaped pressure on Camm over her job performance.

The government came under fire over claims of children in state care sleeping on the floor of government offices, which child protection workers linked to government policies including the cancelling of contracts to some residential care providers.

Camm also came under pressure over budget cuts to domestic and family violence prevention, and a lack of progress on reforms demanded by the former government’s women’s safety and justice taskforce.

Guardian Australia reported that Camm had buried the findings of a panel of domestic and family violence victim-survivors, which was highly critical of police. Her office told one member she was no longer welcome to contact them by phone.

Camm said the attack on Haines had “reinforced the importance of taking concerns about personal health, safety and wellbeing of people in public life very seriously”.

“Public scrutiny and accountability are central to democracy and to our institutions. Harassment, threats, bullying and personal vilification are not. And for the past year this has been my experience. There is much more work to be done.”

The premier, David Crisafulli, said he wanted to “support Amanda” and that she had not been removed over her performance.

It is understood that the government will not instigate a broader reshuffle but will appoint a new face to the ministry to replace Camm.

Among those considered in the frame for a promotion is former senator and Morrison government figure Amanda Stoker, who was elected to the state parliament in 2024.

title: Australia offers astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg for space mission to International Space Station
text:
The federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to the International Space Station.

The mission, slated for 2028, will mark the first time a qualified astronaut has flown to space under the Australian flag.

The ESA offer for Bennell-Pegg to join a future ISS mission garnered support from philanthropists and the Australian space industry, but has previously described by the office of the science minister, Tim Ayres, as “a very expensive undertaking” which no government alone could fund.

Announcing the decision on Friday, Ayres said:“The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost.

“We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6m in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments.”

Bennell-Pegg is director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency (ASA) and completed astronaut training with the ESA in 2024.

She is not the first Australian astronaut, but she is the first to qualify under the Australian flag. Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power, both Australian-born, went to space as US citizens on Nasa missions. Elaine Hyde, a dual Australian and US citizen, last year took a suborbital flight aboard Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin NS-30.

In May, the ASA announced it had entered into “treaty-level discussions” with the ESA, which “would establish a formal framework for enhanced cooperation between Australia and Europe”.

In August, Ayres and the assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, wrote to state and territory leaders asking them to “partner” with the federal government to fund the mission. The letter, according to The Australian, described it as a “complete Australian mission that includes locally developed experiments and ­technology”.

South Australia, where the ASA is headquartered, has publicly committed to supporting Bennell-Pegg’s space bid.

“South Australia stands ready to partner with the commonwealth in what should be a national endeavour,” the premier, Peter Malinauskus, said. “Katherine Bennell-Pegg has the potential to inspire a new generation to dream big and address the single biggest challenge to our economy which is productivity.

“Australia has a massive shortage of young people taking up the fields of science, technology, engineering and maths, and we need more of it if we’re going to grow the nation’s productivity … Nothing would motivate young people more to take up these fields of endeavour than seeing Australia’s first ever flagged astronaut in space.”

A campaign to secure Bennell-Pegg’s spaceflight mission was supported by entrepreneurs Dick Smith and Jim Whalley – who had each pledged $1m funding for the mission – and former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who said on social media that the “project makes long-term econom

title: Rebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10
text:
Rebel Wilson has been ordered to pay A$10 (US$7, £5) in damages after emerging victorious from a bitter legal spat with her latest film’s co-producers.

The Pitch Perfect star directed, co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US.

Filmed on a $22m budget, The Deb made just $335,000 (US$235,000, £175,284) at the local box office and is yet to screen outside Oceania.

Wilson’s co-producers allege that shortfall could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.

The Bridesmaids star claimed in July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money, and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star, Charlotte MacInnes.

The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could buy it from them.

On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden awarded the trio a mere $10 in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons in the New South Wales supreme court.

Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.

Peden awarded her $359,000 (US$251,830, £187,868) plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgment.

Wilson took to Instagram to welcome the victory with a photo of herself in a graduation gown holding a degree from the University of NSW.

“This girl never knew how much she was going to need that law degree!!” she wrote.

“I spoke up because I believed there were serious concerns that needed to be raised on my film The Deb.

“Defending myself has come at an enormous personal, emotional, and financial cost. But I’m proud I stood my ground – for myself and for others I was trying to protect.”

Wilson said she struggled to remain positive throughout the proceedings and thanked her family and followers for their support.

It’s the second victory for Wilson after she was cleared of defaming MacInnes earlier this year following a fiery federal court hearing.

MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.

The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.

MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, saying she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.

That decision is under appeal.

title: CM Satheesan offers to host Raihan Vadra's exhibition in Keralam
text:
Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan has offered to host the exhibition of artist and photographer Raihan Vadra, son of Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, in Keralam, amid a controversy over the removal of some of his photographs depicting Delhi protests.

Raihan Vadra said the Bikaner House administration in Delhi pulled down many of his pictures of the protests at his solo exhibition, 'No Idea Is Final'.

He claimed that the Bikaner House administration had warned him that the exhibition could be cancelled if he did not take down the pictures by 5 p.m. on Wednesday (October 21, 2026).

"Keralam would be happy and proud to host Raihan Vadra's No Idea Is Final exhibition in its entirety. No exclusions, no exceptions," Mr. Satheesan said in a post on X on Thursday (October 23, 2026), tagging Raihan Vadra and Priyanka Gandhi.

Raihan Vadra said on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) that he had shared the exhibition proposal and layout with the Bikaner House management well in advance.

The photographs did not carry any political message but documented protests over the past six months, he had said.

Priyanka Gandhi had strongly criticised the move, saying that those in power who fear artistic expression end up losing the very power they seek to protect.

Calling the removal of the photographs "ridiculous", the Congress MP accused the authorities of "muzzling" the voices of young people across the country.

While a Bikaner House official said the administration was "not authorised to comment" on the matter, the BJP termed the allegations "fake news".

BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari on Thursday said Bikaner House policy did not permit the display of political content and asked Priyanka Gandhi to find another way to "launch" her son into politics.

title: POCSO survivor cannot be denied compensation solely due to absence of injury marks: Allahabad HC
text:
The Allahabad High Court has ruled that a survivor of sexual assault under the POCSO Act cannot be denied compensation merely because the medical report does not record physical injuries.

In the order issued on Thursday (October 22, 2026), a Division Bench of Justice Shekhar B Saraf and Justice Amitabh Kumar Rai directed authorities to pay ₹3 lakh to a minor under the Uttar Pradesh Rani Lakshmi Bai Mahila Samman Kosh scheme within 10 days of the production of a certified copy of the order.

The court held that the district steering committee's decision to withhold compensation was contrary to law and the provisions of the scheme.

Under the scheme, survivors of sexual assault under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act are entitled to compensation of ₹3 lakh. Of this, ₹1 lakh is payable within 15 days of the FIR, while the remaining ₹2 lakh must be paid within a month of the chargesheet being filed.

The case relates to an FIR registered at Sarojini Nagar police station in Lucknow on December 7, 2022. A chargesheet in this connection was filed on January 13, 2023.

The district committee had withheld compensation citing the absence of medical evidence supporting penetrative sexual assault. The state counsel defended the decision, arguing that the medical report did not record injuries indicating penetration.

Rejecting the argument, the High Court observed that physical injury is not a necessary condition for establishing penetrative sexual assault under Section 3 of the POCSO Act.

The Bench held that the absence of injury marks cannot, by itself, negate an allegation of sexual assault. Once the FIR and chargesheet indicate an offence under Section 4 of the Act, compensation cannot be denied solely because the medical report does not record injuries.

Describing the scheme as a beneficial measure intended to alleviate the trauma and suffering of victims, the court said its provisions must be interpreted liberally.

title: Bihar MLC polls begin for 8 seats, 150 candidates in fray
text:
Polling for biennial elections to eight Bihar Legislative Council seats began at 8 a.m. on Friday (October 23, 2026) amid tight security, with 5.32 lakh voters eligible to decide the fate of 150 candidates, officials said.

Voting will continue till 4 p.m. for four Graduates and four Teachers constituencies, they said.

The combined electorate stands at 5,32,847, including 1,46,611 women and 37 third-gender voters, across 933 polling stations. Counting of votes will take place on October 27, they added.

The contest in the Patna Graduates constituency has drawn attention following an open rift within the JD(U), with Mokama MLA Anant Singh backing Jan Suraaj Party candidate Anuj Singh against his own party's nominee, Neeraj Kumar.

Mr. Kumar, a former minister and a close aide of former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar, is seeking a fourth consecutive term from the seat.

Anant Singh has extended support to Anuj Singh, alleging that Neeraj Kumar had worked against him during last year's assembly elections.

Apart from Patna Graduates, the other constituencies going to polls are Darbhanga Graduates, Tirhut Graduates, Kosi Graduates, Patna Teachers, Darbhanga Teachers, Tirhut Teachers and Saran Teachers.

The terms of the sitting MLCs are due to expire on November 16.

The BJP has fielded candidates in four constituencies, including three sitting MLCs seeking re-election, while the JD(U) has nominated candidates for the remaining four seats.

The BJP nominees are MLCs Nawal Kishor Yadav, N. K. Yadav and Sarvesh Kumar, who are seeking re-election from Patna Teachers, Kosi Graduates and Tirhut Graduates, respectively.

The party has also fielded Narendra Kumar Singh from Tirhut Teachers, a seat currently held by Sanjay Kumar Singh of the CPI, a constituent of the opposition INDIA bloc.

The Jan Suraaj Party (JSP), led by Prashant Kishor, is contesting all eight seats. The party revised its candidate list after its initial announcement, replacing Bhushan Jha with Shyam Nandan Yadav in Tirhut Teachers and Ravindra Yadav with Mohammad Imtiyaz (Noorani) in Darbhanga Graduates.

title: What are the powers and functions of Special Executive Magistrates? | Explained
text:
The story so far: A Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court in Delhi accepted the sureties and granted bail to Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on Wednesday (October 21, 2026).

Despite the Delhi Police seeking a three-day extension of custody on law-and-order grounds, Assistant Commissioner of Police Ritu Raj, who presided over the proceedings, ordered their release. CJP activists had challenged the legality of their continued detention. The case has brought into focus the roles and powers of SEMs and their differences from judicial magistrates and their authority to impose preventive measures.

Who is a Special Executive Magistrate?

State governments appoint SEMs for specific areas or purposes and give them the powers exercised by the Executive Magistrates under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023. It is dealt under Section 15.

While Executive Magistrates perform continued administrative and preventive functions, SEMs are appointed for a specified period, area or function, such as particular situations that require preventive action or maintenance of public order. Their powers also depend on the authority conferred on them by the State government.

What is the function of SEMs?

The powers of SEMs are intended to allow authorities to intervene when there is a likelihood of disturbance rather than responding after the offence has occurred. They maintain public order and prevent breaches of peace by performing preventive and administrative functions.

The Executive Magistrate can require a person who is likely to cause a breach of peace or disturb public tranquillity to show cause why they should not execute a bond to keep the peace. So, depending on the circumstances, they may be required to furnish a bond for a specified period. It is subject to the procedure established by law. This is dealt under Section 126 of the BNSS.

Executive Magistrates can also exercise powers under Section 163 of the BNSS to issue urgent orders in case of nuisance or apprehended danger. It is likely to prevent, or tends to prevent, obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed, or danger to human life, health or safety or a disturbance of the public tranquillity, or a riot, or an affray.

Preventive arrest can be made by police officers when necessary to prevent the commission of a cognisable offence that cannot otherwise be prevented, according to Section 170 of the BNSS. This is a police power, not exclusively that of SEMs.

The police initiated a preventive proceeding against the CJP activists, alleging that they had breached peace bonds that they had signed. SEM extended their custody on October 19, citing concerns about public peace. Later on Wednesday (October 21), their sureties were accepted, and they were released on an undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar while it remained a denotified protest site.

title: Why are Andhra Pradesh’s civic poll nominations under the Supreme Court’s scrutiny? | Explained
text:
The story so far:

The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP)’s allegation of obstructions during the filing of nominations for elections to urban local bodies (ULBs) has landed the State Election Commission (SEC) in a tight spot, and the process has come under the Supreme Court’s scrutiny. The focus has now shifted from political claims to the SEC’s ability to establish a level playing field.

The question in Andhra Pradesh’s municipal elections is no longer only who will win the civic bodies. It is also whether every eligible candidate gets a fair opportunity to enter the contest. The Supreme Court’s intervention, following a petition by the YSRCP, has come at a critical stage of the electoral process.

By directing the Commission to examine complaints of alleged obstruction, consider extending nomination deadlines wherever it finds candidates were unable to file papers because of the law-and-order situation, and defer publication of the final candidates’ list till October 25, the court has made it clear that adherence to an election calendar cannot, by itself, settle concerns about electoral fairness.

The court’s directions do not establish the YSRCP’s allegations as true. They do, however, require the authorities to examine whether any candidate was denied the opportunity to contest because of a breakdown in law and order.

What does the YSRCP allege?

The YSRCP approached the Supreme Court after the Andhra Pradesh High Court declined, on October 18, to extend the nomination deadline. The party had first approached the High Court before the nomination process began, seeking preventive measures over its apprehensions of violence. A single judge declined omnibus relief on October 15 but gave individual candidates liberty to approach the election officers concerned for remedial action.

The opposition party alleged that its candidates had been assaulted, threatened, obstructed from reaching nomination centres and, in some instances, deprived of their nomination papers. Before the Supreme Court, the YSRCP’s counsel claimed that nearly two-thirds, or about 63%, of its candidates were prevented from filing nominations, a claim the State strongly contested. The nomination period for the ULB elections ran from October 16 to October 18.

The YSRCP’s petition cited alleged incidents in Punganur, Rayachoti, Kadapa and Tirupati, including the alleged snatching and tearing of a candidate’s nomination papers in Kadapa and the alleged prevention of nine candidates from entering Returning Officers’ offices in Tirupati. It also referred to an alleged attack on the convoy of YSRCP MP P.V. Midhun Reddy.

The political significance is considerable. In local elections, where a candidate’s personal network, caste equations, local influence and access to party machinery can be decisive, preventing a rival from entering the race can be more effective than defeating that rival at the polling booth.

title: What does eMudhra’s web security key leak mean for internet users? | Explained
text:
The story so far: Eight private keys used to issue web security certificates by Bengaluru-headquartered eMudhra Ltd were exposed, it emerged on Tuesday (October 20, 2026). The incident has prompted an advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team, India (CERT-in) and immediate patches from developers of major web browsers. eMudhra’s services are used across several government and public sector bank websites.

The internet relies on a small number of so-called “root” certifying authorities (CAs) who can then authorise intermediate CAs to issue SSL certificates for webpages. Those SSL certificates are on practically every website, acting as an assurance that a website is what it claims to represent. This system works on trust, and only a handful of root CAs are trusted by browsers around the world. eMudhra operates one of these trusted CAs.

title: ‘Game boards’ carved on rocks in Kasaragod hint at age-old yen for leisure
text:
Rock-carved game boards resembling the traditional 14-pit Manjadippala or Kadippala boards used in Kerala have been discovered at Madikkai Umichi, Banam, and Cheemeni Ariyittapara in Kasaragod district, providing possible evidence that people in the region engaged in recreational activities thousands of years ago.

Six distinct game boards have been identified so far; four at Banam; one at Umichi in Madikkai; and one Ariyittapara at Cheemeni. All of them are located near the natural water reservoirs, locally known as Pallam, in Kasaragod district.

The discovery suggests that the inhabitants of the region had opportunities for recreation and possessed an understanding of counting and numerical relationships, observed Nandakumar Koroth, head of the Department of History at the Nehru Arts and Science College, Kanhangad. The finding emerged after archeology enthusiast Satheesan Kaliyana drew attention to unusual pits carved into rocks in the area.

“The rock carvings indicate that people who lived in these areas may have played games during their leisure time. The resemblance between these ancient structures and the traditional Manjadikkali boards used by people till about 40 years ago is particularly significant,” said Dr. Koroth.

Need for conservation

He said they could have been made using stone tools such as celts or iron tools. But further archaeological investigation and scientific dating are required to establish their precise age. The State Archaeology department or the Archaeological Survey Of India should intervene to document and protect the rock-carved boards, the researchers said adding that conservation is urgent because several carvings have already been buried or are located in areas affected by construction and proposed development projects.

Senior archaeologist and former archaeology professor Ajith Kumar, however, cautioned against assigning a specific antiquity to the carvings without further evidence. While the structures could be identified as game boards resembling Pallankuzhi, their discovery near other archaeological remains did not establish that they belonged to the same period.

He said Pallankuzhi is a traditional game played on a board containing two parallel rows of pits usually seven in each row. Some boards have larger pits that serve particular functions in the game. Seeds, including tamarind seeds, are traditionally used as counters. Dr. Ajith said game boards of this kind are not confined to Kasaragod or Kerala.

Similar examples have been reported at several archaeological sites in south India, including Tamil Nadu and parts of Karnataka. Similar structures have been documented on dark volcanic basalt rock at Deccan College in Pune, its nearby temple premises and the Aurangabad cave complex. Archaeologist have also identified comparable Mancala boards in Africa with some believed to date back approximately 8,000 years.

title: How India thwarted Pakistan’s bid to steal crucial defence data
text:
About six months ago, a team of officers in Andhra Pradesh’s Counter Intelligence Cell (CIC) noticed an unusual pattern of messaging across various social media platforms, including interactive messaging applications such as WhatsApp.

What intrigued the officers was an abnormal frequency of incoming and outgoing international communications. The communication pattern was immediately red-flagged. The CIC team alerted central intelligence agencies and leveraged the resources of NATGRID (National Intelligence Grid) and CMS (Central Monitoring System) ֪— core components of India’s security infrastructure designed to combat terrorism, espionage, and cross-border threats — to trace Internet Protocol (IP) logs and WhatsApp One-Time Password (OTP) sharing patterns.

title: A greying population, a strained care system
text:
Girija (name changed) spent years working as a domestic worker before her failing knees made it difficult for her to continue. Hoping to find a more manageable way to earn a living, the 60-year-old borrowed money from acquaintances and set up a roadside vegetable stall. But another health problem emerged, making it difficult to keep the business running.

“She learnt that she was suffering from urinary incontinence. Taking frequent loo breaks while managing the stall was not practical, and she eventually decided to shut shop, losing her source of income in the process,” says Gurajada Sobha Pernidevi, founder-president of Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, a voluntary organisation working for the welfare of women.

For older people with limited financial means, a health problem can do more than cause physical discomfort; it can take away their livelihood, independence and opportunities to socialise. Conditions that are difficult to discuss, such as urinary incontinence, are often endured in silence because of embarrassment and the cost of managing them.

Unlike ailments that call for joint replacement surgery or a cardiac stent, these less visible difficulties of ageing often receive scant attention, despite their potential to disrupt daily life. However, as Telangana’s share of elderly population grows, addressing such overlooked needs will become increasingly important.

Telangana’s population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 12.5% in 2026 to 17.1% in 2036, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s report, ‘State Finances — A Study of Budgets of 2025-26: Demographic Transition in India — Implications for State Finances’.

The State is expected to join the category of ageing ones, where senior citizens account for at least 15% of the population. The projected demographic shift raises questions about how healthcare, caregiving and community support can keep pace with the needs of older people, particularly those who live alone or cannot afford private services.

Associations working with senior citizens say the challenges range from obtaining medicines and reaching hospitals to finding dependable caregivers and accessing mental health support.

P. Shyam Kumar, State project coordinator at HelpAge India, says doorstep medical services, including palliative care, could make healthcare more accessible. Nutritional supplements and the delivery of medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists could also help older people manage their health.

“Without adequate support, their condition may deteriorate, leading to more hospital visits, additional expenses and greater dependence on family members. So, supplying medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists may work in this direction,” he adds.

title: Cabinet Secretary had copied acknowledgement sent to letters by two ECs to CEC for ‘information’: RTI reply
text:
Days after two Election Commissioners (ECs) S.S. Sandhu and Vivek Joshi wrote to Cabinet Secretary T.V. Somanathan on July 29 regarding the working of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg, the secretariat sent an acknowledgment to both with a copy to Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar for his “information”, a Right to Information (RTI) response has revealed.

The Cabinet Secretariat noted that the letters were from the ECs in their individual capacity and while needed to be taken with seriousness, cannot be taken as formal communication from the Election Commission of India (ECI) as a whole. In the absence of any official communication from the commission any action can be construed as “interference”.

The RTI plea was filed by Commodore (retired) Lokesh Batra.

Work allocation

A Cabinet Secretariat file noting dated August 3 says both the ECs had stated that Mr. Garg, after assuming the charge as link officer of DEC (Administration), issued an order regarding work allocation of equivalent and senior officers to him without discussing the revised work allocation with the commission or the officers concerned. Further, the ECs stated that this happened despite repeated oral and written instructions to all officers against taking such actions without prior discussion/approval of the commission.

“In this connection, we may request the Chief Election Commissioner for his opinion on the issue. Accordingly, a draft D.O. is put up for approval, please,” it said.

However, the very next day, that is August 4, the file notes that “the commission is a constitutional body and is insulated from executive interference by design to ensure that it functions independently and in a transparent manner”.

“The above communications are from the ECs in their individual capacity and, while they must be taken with due seriousness, they cannot be seen as a formal communication from the commission as a whole”.

It further says the ECs have sent these communications for appropriate action. However, “in the absence of any official communication from the commission as a whole, any action at this stage may be inappropriate. It may also be construed as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body”.

And hence, it will be appropriate to send acknowledgement to both ECs with a copy to PPS to the CEC for “information of CEC”.

A copy was also marked to be sent to the Secretary, Department of Personnel and Training since Mr. Garg was an All-India Service officer as well as ACC appointee.

“Draft DO may be put up accordingly”, it said.

Subsequently, on August 5, Mr. Somanathan wrote to both the ECs acknowledging the letters with a copy to PPS to the CEC.

It was though not clear from the RTI responses whether Mr. Gyanesh Kumar had in any manner responded to or acknowledged the information received from the Cabinet Secretariat.

title: Indian killed as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport
text:
Two people, including an Indian national, were killed and eight others injured on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) in a Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil hub, the kingdom’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said.

The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed the Indian national’s death. “Saudi authorities have informed that one Indian national was among two people who unfortunately lost their lives in the attack on Dammam airport yesterday night and two Indian nationals were injured,” the Indian embassy wrote in a social media post on Thursday (October 22, 2026). “We are ascertaining further details and contacting the affected families. Our thoughts and prayers are with the family and loved ones of the deceased and we wish speedy recovery of the injured.”

Airport operations and air traffic had returned to normal after brief disruptions, the Saudi aviation authority said.

Separately, the Houthis (Ansar Allah) claimed that Saudi Arabia had attacked a yacht carrying Indians in the Red Sea, adding that they were conducting rescue operations.

The Houthis, who control northern and northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sana’a, said they launched missile and drone attacks at the Saudi Ministry of Defence in Riyadh and the Dammam airport. They also struck a facility of Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned petroleum and natural gas company, in Yanbu, and the Abha International Airport in the southwest.

If Saudi Arabia continues to attack Yemen, “we will resort to major options we did not want to take, and we hold it responsible for the consequences,” the militants said, according to the Houthi-aligned Almasirah television.

The Iran-aligned rebels, who captured Sana’a in 2014 and expanded their territorial control along Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast last month, also claimed that the Saudi forces on Thursday targeted an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island in Red Sea, carrying 14 Indians.

“The [Houthi] Armed Forces are carrying out rescue operations for those on board, with further details to be provided later,” they said, according to Almasirah. “It indicated that this reckless behavior by the Saudi enemy threatens international navigation in the Red Sea, requiring the international community to stop the Saudi enemy from these reckless actions.”

The targeting of a civilian vessel carrying Indian nationals raises serious concerns about the safety of international navigation and the potential for civilian casualties, they added.

Saudi Arabia started bombing Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis captured Sana’a a few months earlier. In 2022, Riyadh and the Houthi leadership agreed to a ceasefire as part of a broader Iran-Saudi rapprochement. title: Face-off with China continues at multiple locations along Arunachal border: ITBP D-G
text:
Confrontations with Chinese troops continue to take place at multiple sites along the border in Arunachal Pradesh, according to Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) director general Shatrujeet Kapur.

“In the past few-days, a situation arose where face-off happened at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues,” Mr. Kapur said on Thursday.

This is the first official confirmation of the scale of the rising tensions on the north-eastern border since July this year.

Also Read | India, China to push for ‘early and substantial harvest’ of border delimitation

High-altitude commandos

Speaking at the Himveer Samman Samaroah, an annual felicitation ceremony for ITBP personnel, Mr. Kapur said ITBP commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the Arunachal border.

“Our newly raised Shaurya commandos played an exemplary role in this. ITBP was raised as a mountain guerilla force and we were given border guarding duty along China in 2004,” he said. “We need not leave our original function, and a specialised high altitude mountain fighting force is being set up, distinct than the army. We will soon have one full battalion of Shaurya commandos; high-altitude [deployment] is our strength,” Mr. Kapur added, during the event held at the Central Training College (CTC), Alwar, Rajasthan.

Also Read | India, China open door to clarifying LAC perceptions

Chinese troops dig in

Government sources told The Hindu that since late July, India and China have been engaged in a stand-off at Asaphila near Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh. The Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have pitched their tents at an elevation, within 6 km to 7 km of India’s perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), near the Maja company operating base in Taksing circle of Upper Subansiri district, sources said.

“Sometime in July, during routine patrolling, Indian and Chinese troops came face to face near Maja. After brief confrontation, both sides returned but the Chinese PLA came back in larger number few days later and pitched tents, around 6-7 kms within India’s perception of the LAC,” the source said.

India has also increased deployment along the border.

title: The grandmothers hitting patriarchy and weights
text:
Period blood is the only blood that does not flow because of violence. “Still, society despises that blood the most.” Savitri Hooda, 65, speaks straight into her phone camera, standing under a neem tree in her home’s backyard. That video, shot from Rohtak’s Mungan village, 70 km north-west of Delhi, got 19,000 ‘likes’ on Instagram.

In another reel, she looks at the camera and calls her own generation “shoddy”. “Should I list their misdeeds? They killed daughters in the womb, discriminated against their own daughters, burnt their daughters-in-law for dowry, and leered at other women. They treated women as second-class citizens and now cannot stand their freedom.” That got her 4,87,000 likes and a whole lot of comments from people showering love on “Dadi”.

Savitri Hooda

Welcome to @tai_savitri’s month-old Instagram account, which has just 27 posts but 3,08,000 followers. Her bio says: “Desi feminist from Haryana. Freedom and unfiltered opinions.”

The overwhelming response to her profile has been startling even for the family. Her son, Ashish, recalls receiving the first podcast invitation when Savitri had around 3,000 followers. After her video on mental health went viral last month, interview requests began pouring in.

Across the National Capital Region (NCR), women over 60 are putting their voices out on social media. They are singing, dancing, and giving out wisdom that the youth is lapping up.

The irreverent feminist

For Savitri, speaking her mind is hardly new. The rebellious streak that now finds an audience online surfaced when she was a schoolgirl. She dropped out in Class 7 after her mother, whom she describes as “very conservative”, refused to let her participate in a school play about dowry and opposed her taking up judo as well. “She thought it would disgrace the family. So I quit my studies in protest,” Savitri says.

It is a decision she still regrets.

Her formal education may have ended early, but Ashish says his mother has always been receptive to new ideas. She listens, reflects, and frequently brings her own observations into discussions, sometimes surprising the family with the connections she makes.

Her curiosity has also translated into considerable digital independence. Savitri records and uploads videos, manages her YouTube account and responds to comments herself. She uses the voice-to-text tool because it is faster than entering text manually. “If someone writes in English and I cannot understand the comment, I reply, ‘Thank you for sharing your views’,” she says.

To meet her is to meet an anti-influencer. She sits cross-legged on a bed in a dimly lit room, plaster peeling off its green-painted walls. Clothes hang shabbily on pegs. Ashish, an aspiring stand-up comic and novelist, leaning against a pillow beside her. She asks her husband to make three cups of tea. “What is the point in talking about feminism if I cannot finish patriarchy at my own house?” she says, chuckling.

title: An ironclad resolve in the national interest
text:
Some forces that cannot bear to see India’s rapid march towards becoming a developed nation have become increasingly active in the country. Their intention is to deliberately poison the national atmosphere and create instability. As a result, the internal security challenges confronting India have become increasingly complex. Just as violent protests erupted in Nepal and Bangladesh, certain anti-national elements have begun speaking of triggering similar agitations in India. With the support of some foreign powers, Opposition parties are talking about a ‘regime change’. Attempts are being made to undermine democracy and threaten the Constitution authored under the stewardship of Bharat Ratna Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar. Efforts are also under way to fuel extremism in the country. Drug trafficking, which threatens to derail the lives of young people, is on the rise. Misinformation spread through social media and attempts to create social discord pose a serious threat to India’s social harmony.

However, no such instability will be allowed to take root in India, nor will the sinister designs of foreign powers be permitted to succeed. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, our country’s formidable Home Minister Amit Shah is ensuring that this does not happen. The era when security agencies would scramble to respond only after an incident had occurred is long past. We are now in an era defined by Mr. Shah’s firm, farsighted, swift, direct, and comprehensive decision-making. That is why the citizens of India need not fear any such attempts at destabilisation. Whatever may be happening elsewhere in the world, India remains a nation governed by the Constitution of Dr. Ambedkar. No one will succeed in pushing the country into anarchy. Mr. Shah celebrated his birthday on Thursday. While extending my birthday wishes to him, I pray to the Almighty to grant him the strength to maintain India’s internal security at the highest level and effectively counter anti-national elements.

Historic decisions

When comparing India before 2014 with India after 2014, one cannot look merely at the change of political power. One must also consider the country’s development aspirations, its approach to national security, the pace of infrastructure creation, India’s position on the global stage, and its willingness to resolve long-pending issues. Mr. Modi’s leadership gave a new direction to the aspirations of the nation while Mr. Shah strengthened this journey through his organisational capabilities, political planning, and support for key decisions. Together, the Prime Minister’s farsighted vision and his colleague’s ability to implement it provide an important example of how transformative change can be achieved.

title: SEBI cautions investors against fraudulent stock-tip WhatsApp groups
text:
Markets regulator SEBI on Thursday (October 22, 2026) cautioned investors against fraudulent WhatsApp stock-tip groups that use 'astroturfing' — fake endorsements and profit claims — to create a false impression of credibility and lure investors.

In a statement, SEBI said certain unregistered persons were offering stock recommendations to investors through invitation-only WhatsApp groups in the name of free investor education. The operators of these fraudulent groups often use overseas WhatsApp numbers posing as market experts.

“To make these calls look credible, certain members, acting in concert with the operators, post false claims of profit and praise the 'expert'. This practice, known as astroturfing, creates a false impression of genuine support and induces unsuspecting investors to act on the call,” SEBI said.

The regulator also highlighted a tactic used by such groups after enforcement agencies or regulatory bodies take action against them.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) noted that members are often contacted from a new number and invited to join another group, with operators claiming that the previous group had been banned due to social media platform restrictions.

One such message cited by SEBI reads, "Due to the social media platform's risk control measures, our previous group has been banned. This new group will provide daily recommendations of quality stock information and trading guidance. Please join the group.”

Advising investors to exercise caution, SEBI said they should not join invitation-only WhatsApp groups operated by unknown persons or individuals claiming to be stock market experts, particularly those using overseas numbers.

Investors have also been advised not to be influenced by messages containing praise, profit claims or trade confirmations posted by other members, as such posts could be planted to create a misleading impression.

The regulator said messages claiming that a group had been suspended, closed or banned, and inviting members to join a new group should be treated as red flags.

It further advised investors against opening accounts on, or transferring money to, trading platforms or applications recommended by such groups. ​Investors should also refrain from sharing their investment holdings or trading account details with the operators, the regulator advised.

“Deal only with SEBI-registered intermediaries and use only authentic trading apps,” the regulator said, adding that investors could verify the registration status of intermediaries through its official website.

SEBI said the statement was intended to caution investors against acting on stock tips and trading calls circulated through such closed fraudulent WhatsApp groups and urged them to remain vigilant while dealing in the securities market.

title: BJP President Nitin Nabin on a three-day visit to Jharkhand from October 23
text:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) National President Nitin Nabin will be on a three-day visit to Jharkhand starting October 23. He will participate in the inaugural session of the Jharkhand BJP State Working Committee meeting, which will begin on October 24.

The state unit of the BJP has finalised all arrangements for his visit, and there is great enthusiasm among party workers regarding the National President’s visit. State capital, Ranchi, has been decorated with BJP flags, banners and his cutout to welcome him.

Jharkhand BJP State President Aditya Sahu on Thursday (October 22, 2026) held a meeting with party office-bearers at the state office to review the preparations for the National President’s visit and his welcome.

The meeting was attended by State Vice-Presidents Balmukund Sahay and Rakesh Prasad; General Secretary (Organization) Pawan Sai; State General Secretaries Ganesh Mishra, Amar Kumar Bauri, and Manoj Singh and others.

State General Secretary Amar Kumar Bauri said that it will be Nitin Nabin’s second visit to Jharkhand, the sacred land of ‘Dharti Aaba’ Bhagwan Birsa Munda—since assuming the role of National President. He added that party workers are particularly enthusiastic about his visit.

Mr. Bauri mentioned that the Mr. Nabin is scheduled to reach Ranchi Airport at 7:00 PM on October 23 and arrangements have been made to welcome him with traditional Jharkhandi customs, including the playing of drums and a shower of flower petals.

“Party workers will also welcome him at various locations across the capital. During his stay, he will attend the inaugural session of the State Working Committee meeting on October 24, where he will provide key guidance to party office-bearers and workers,”Mr. Bauri said.

A senior leader of the Jharkhand BJP asserted that during his visit, he will hold meetings with senior state-level leaders Members of Parliament (MPs), Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs), and party workers to discuss the future strategy. The BJP leader added that these meetings will serve to review the organization’s ongoing work, and roadmap for upcoming political and organisational activities.

The meeting scheduled for October 25 will focus on key issues such as strengthening the organization, ensuring the active engagement of party workers at the booth level, and effectively disseminating information about the central government’s schemes to the general public.

“Discussion is also likely to take place on ‘Mission 2029’, the next assembly election in Jharkhand. Potential candidates for the Giridih by-election will also be discussed, “the BJP leader said.

Giridih assembly seat has fallen vacant after the death of Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM) MLA Sudviya Kumar.

title: Congress MLAs burn Punjab CM effigy over poor law-and-order following anti-drugs crusaders murder
text:
The Punjab Assembly on Thursday (October 23, 2026), during the obituary references, paid tributes to anti-drug crusader Parvinder Singh Jhota, who was shot at in Punjab’s Mansa, even as, before the commencement of the session, Congress MLAs led by the leader of the Opposition, Partap Singh Bajwa, burned the effigy of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, demanding his resignation, outside the Punjab Assembly complex.

Mr. Bajwa said the Chief Minister, who also holds the Home portfolio, has completely failed to maintain law and order in the State. The broad daylight murder of Jhota, who raised his voice against the drug menace, is a glaring example of the government’s failure.

Outside the Assembly, speaking to journalists, Mr. Bajwa said “It is the voice of the entire Punjab that law and order has completely ended in Punjab. No person’s life is safe in this State, no one’s business is safe, no one’s work is safe, no one’s family is safe. So, we are asking for Bhagwant Mann’s resignation.”

Separately, Punjab Bharatiya Janata Party president Kewal Singh Dhillon hit out at the State government, accusing it of running away from its accountability. “This was evident from the fact that the Punjab Assembly session today lasted only a few minutes, during which neither Punjab’s concerns were discussed nor were any deliberations held on the issues facing the State,” he said in a statement.

Mr. Dhillon added, “The government will have to answer on issues surrounding the drug menace, gangsterism, extortion and the deteriorating law-and-order situation. The people of Punjab are demanding answers from the AAP government regarding the deaths of Parminder Singh Jhota, Bikramjit Singh, Gulzar Singh and others, who lost their lives for raising their voice against drug menace.”

Mr. Dhillon said that Home Minister Amit Shah had reiterated his commitment to eliminate drugs from Punjab at their roots and had also asserted that an NDA government would be formed in Punjab. “This meant that the BJP would form the government in 2027 in Punjab,” he said.

title: Bihar Council elections today; Patna Graduates’ seat in focus as JD(U) faces internal tussle
text:
Ahead of Friday’s biennial elections to eight seats of the Bihar Legislative Council, State JD(U) president Umesh Kushwaha and party MLC Sanjay Kumar Singh on Thursday met Patna Graduates’ seat candidate Neeraj Kumar for a closed-door meeting.

The seat, from which Mr. Neeraj is seeking a fourth consecutive term, has become the centre of attention after JD(U)’s Mokama MLA Anant Singh declared support for Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) candidate Anuj Kumar Singh.

Mr. Anant claimed that Mr. Neeraj had opposed him in every Assembly election held in Mokama.

Polling for the four Graduates’ and four Teachers’ constituencies will be held from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Counting is scheduled for October 27. The terms of the sitting MLCs are set to expire on November 16.

The ruling allies BJP and JD(U) are contesting four seats each while the JSP is contesting all eight.

Bid to placate

The JD(U) twice tried to broker peace between Mr. Anant and Mr. Neeraj. It had tasked Munger MP and Union Panchayati Raj Minister Rajiv Ranjan Singh alias Lalan Singh to mediate. Mr. Lalan later said Mr. Anant had “reservations and grudges which the party should have addressed earlier”.

Former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar, Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary and Deputy Chief Minister Vijay Kumar Sinha had visited Mr. Neeraj after he was admitted to a private hospital on Monday for heart-related issues.

“I am not aware of what is going on for the election as my workers have taken the mantle on my behalf. I will go and find out,” Mr. Neeraj said after he was discharged on Wednesday.

title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
text:
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.

The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.

The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.

Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.

Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.

"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."

The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.

Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.

In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.

But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.

UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.

The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.

The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.

title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
text:
Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US PresidentDonald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.

Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.

Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks.

Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back."

The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.

The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.

Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.

Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."

He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."

The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.

The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.

The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.

The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.

BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.

Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.

Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions.

The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
text:
From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.

They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.

When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.

What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.

"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."

As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."

By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.

Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.

Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.

The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.

Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.

The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.

Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.

The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.

The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.

Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.

We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.

"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."

Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.
